toD() caches the resolved Endpoint/Producer per distinct URI it computes (via the producer cache) so that a repeated destination doesn't pay endpoint-resolution cost every message; the cacheSize option bounds how many distinct resolved endpoints/producers stay cached (0 = the default cache size, a negative value disables caching entirely). A highly dynamic URI (a queue name keyed by, say, per-order tenant ID with unbounded cardinality) can grow this cache without bound if left at defaults, which is the operational reason cacheSize exists.

The YAML DSL expresses the same choice/when/otherwise structure structurally rather than as chained method calls: a choice step holds a when list (each with its own predicate expression and its own steps) and an optional otherwise block with its own steps — there's no .end()/.endChoice() distinction in YAML because indentation, not method chaining, marks where a block ends.

snippets.note: the canonical choice()/when()/otherwise() shape; branches tested top to bottom, first match wins
filter() drops silently — contrast with validate() (Chapter 11), which throws
destination URI computed per exchange from a header; cacheSize bounds how many resolved endpoints/producers stay cached

snippets.code:
- from:
    uri: direct:orders
    steps:
      - choice:
          when:
            - simple: "${header.OrderType} == 'DOMESTIC'"
              steps:
                - to: direct:domesticOrders
            - simple: "${header.OrderType} == 'INTERNATIONAL'"
              steps:
                - to: direct:internationalOrders
          otherwise:
            steps:
              - to: direct:unroutedOrders
snippets.note: same choice/when/otherwise structure in the YAML DSL — structural nesting, no .end()/.endChoice()

pitfalls: Forgetting otherwise() and assuming an unmatched message is an error — by default it silently falls through the choice block with no branch run and no exception.
Ordering when() branches so a broader/earlier predicate shadows a later, more specific one — evaluation is top-to-bottom, first-match-wins, so the more specific check must come first.

Nesting an EIP that needs its own .end() (e.g. loadBalance()) directly inside a when()/otherwise() and closing it with a plain .end() instead of .endChoice() — this closes the wrong scope and the next when()/otherwise() call won't compile against the Choice.
Confusing filter()'s silent drop with validate()'s (Chapter 11) thrown exception — swapping one for the other changes whether a rejected message disappears quietly or triggers exception-handling.
Leaving toD() at its default cache size against a destination URI with effectively unbounded cardinality (e.g. keyed by customer ID), letting the endpoint/producer cache grow without bound.

claims.text: The Splitter EIP (split()) breaks one incoming Exchange into many sub-Exchanges. Each sub-exchange is a copy of the original exchange with the body replaced by one part of the split result, so headers and properties set before the split are visible to every part.

split() accepts any Expression to decide how to cut the body up: tokenize(...) for delimited text (e.g. one line per message), xpath(...) for an XML node-set, jsonpath(...) for a JSON array, or simply body() when the body is already a java.util.Collection/array/Iterable/Iterator, which Camel splits element by element automatically with no extra expression needed.

By default split() runs non-streaming: it first materializes the full list of parts (so the total count is known up front), then processes each part in turn, holding all parts in memory. streaming() switches to on-demand splitting that produces and processes one part at a time without materializing the whole list first, trading lower memory use for not knowing the total part count in advance.

If split() is given no explicit AggregationStrategy, Camel defaults to UseLatestAggregationStrategy: the last sub-exchange processed simply becomes the outgoing exchange after the split() block, and every earlier sub-exchange's result is discarded. Without an explicit strategy, split() is a fan-out that throws away everything except whatever the final part produced.

Supplying a custom AggregationStrategy to split() lets each processed sub-exchange fold into a running result exchange inline, before the split() block completes. This inline recombination is a different mechanism from the standalone Aggregator EIP (aggregate()): it only ever combines the parts of the one exchange that was just split, in the same block, on the same thread of control (or a bounded set of parallel threads) as the split itself.

parallelProcessing() on split() processes sub-exchanges concurrently, but the calling thread still blocks at the split() block until every sub-exchange has finished before the route continues past it — parallelProcessing changes how the parts are processed, not whether the caller waits. When combined with a custom AggregationStrategy, that strategy's aggregate() method may then be invoked concurrently from multiple threads and must be implemented thread-safe; Camel synchronizes calls to aggregate() by default so it is safe (if serialized) even without that guarantee.

The Aggregator EIP (aggregate()) solves a different problem from split()'s inline recombination: it correlates and combines separate incoming Exchanges — which can arrive from many different route invocations over time, not necessarily from one split() call — into a single completed Exchange, grouped by a correlation Expression evaluated per exchange.

aggregate()'s AggregationStrategy has the same aggregate(Exchange oldExchange, Exchange newExchange) shape used by split(): oldExchange is null on the first exchange seen for a given correlation key (the strategy typically just returns newExchange to start the group), and on every later exchange for that same key, oldExchange holds the running aggregate built so far.

A correlation group completes — releasing its aggregated exchange downstream — under whichever configured completion condition fires first: completionSize(n) after n exchanges have joined that key; completionTimeout(ms), an inactivity timeout that resets every time a new exchange arrives for that key; completionInterval(ms), a fixed periodic sweep that completes whatever has accumulated regardless of per-key activity; or completionPredicate(...), evaluated against the aggregated exchange after each new arrival. completionTimeout and completionInterval cannot both be configured at the same time, but either can be combined with completionSize — whichever condition trips first wins for that key.

Aggregated state lives in a pluggable AggregationRepository. Camel's default is an in-memory repository, which loses every in-flight (not-yet-completed) group if the process restarts. A production aggregator that must survive a restart plugs in a persistent AggregationRepository implementation instead — Camel ships JDBC-, Infinispan-, and similar-backed options.

forceCompletionOnStop tells the aggregator to complete and release every in-flight group when the CamelContext stops, instead of leaving partially-aggregated groups stranded in the repository with no consumer left to complete them.

snippets.note: tokenize() splits a newline-delimited body into one sub-exchange per line; verified against the Splitter EIP reference (Camel 4.18.x).
split()'s own AggregationStrategy recombines the parts of one split message inline, in the same block — distinct from the standalone aggregate() EIP.
aggregate() correlates separately-arriving exchanges by header("orderId"); completionSize and completionTimeout are combined so whichever fires first releases the group.

pitfalls: split() without an explicit AggregationStrategy defaults to UseLatestAggregationStrategy, which silently keeps only the last sub-exchange's result and discards every earlier one — easy to miss because the route compiles and runs without error, it just quietly loses data.

Conflating split()'s inline AggregationStrategy with the standalone Aggregator EIP: the former only recombines the pieces of the one message just split, in one block; the latter correlates separate exchanges arriving over time by a correlation key. Reaching for aggregate() when split()'s own strategy would do (or vice versa) solves the wrong problem.

completionTimeout and completionInterval cannot both be set on the same aggregate() — they are two different notions of "done" (per-key inactivity vs. fixed periodic sweep) and picking the wrong one changes when a group actually completes.

Shipping the default in-memory AggregationRepository to production: any in-flight (not yet completed) correlation group is lost if the process restarts, silently dropping partially-aggregated data with no error at the time of loss.

claims.text: Multicast (Camel's multicast() EIP) sends a copy of one incoming exchange to a fixed set of endpoints declared right in the route — the destinations are the .to() calls chained inside the multicast() block, baked into the route's source and identical for every message that passes through.

Recipient List (Camel's recipientList() EIP) sends a copy of one incoming exchange to a set of endpoints computed at runtime from an expression evaluated per exchange (commonly a header). If the expression's result is a String, Camel splits it into individual endpoint URIs on a delimiter (default a comma, re-configurable, e.g. recipientList(header("targets"), ";")), trimming whitespace around each URI; if the expression already evaluates to a List/Collection of URIs, Camel uses it directly with no string-splitting step.

Camel's own documentation describes Multicast as the baseline implementation that both the Recipient List and the Splitter EIPs are built on — the same underlying processor, the same core option set (parallelProcessing, stopOnException, aggregationStrategy, timeout, streaming), and the same AggregationStrategy.aggregate(oldExchange, newExchange) contract apply to all three; they differ in what gets multicast (a fixed endpoint list, a runtime-computed endpoint list, or the parts of one already-split body) rather than in the machinery that fans a message out and folds results back.

By default multicast() (and recipientList()) processes its destinations sequentially, on the calling thread, in declared/list order. parallelProcessing() switches to running the destinations concurrently on Camel's executor service (a default one, or a custom executorService() you supply) — but the calling thread still blocks at the multicast/recipientList block until every destination has finished, the same "parallel changes how the parts run, not whether the route waits" shape as split()'s parallelProcessing().

Left with no explicit AggregationStrategy, multicast() and recipientList() both default to keeping only the last destination's reply as the outgoing exchange once the block finishes — every earlier destination's result (and any exception attached to it) is silently discarded, the same UseLatestAggregationStrategy-shaped quiet drop that split() defaults to without a strategy.

stopOnException (default false) controls what happens when one destination throws: left at its default, Camel still sends to every remaining destination even after one has failed, records the exception on that destination's own exchange, and (with an AggregationStrategy in place) leaves it to that strategy's aggregate() to inspect newExchange.getException() per branch and decide how to react. Setting stopOnException(true) instead aborts the whole multicast/recipientList the moment any one destination throws, and propagates that exception straight to the route's error handler.

Recipient List carries two options multicast has no use for, both consequences of its destinations being computed rather than fixed: ignoreInvalidEndpoints() skips a runtime-computed URI that doesn't resolve to a real endpoint instead of failing the whole exchange, and cacheSize bounds how many distinct dynamically-resolved endpoint producers Camel's ProducerCache keeps warm — important because, unlike multicast's handful of literal .to() calls, a recipient list can compute a different set of destination URIs on every single message.

Recipient List and Dynamic To (toD(), covered in the Content-Based Routing chapter) solve adjacent but distinct problems: toD() computes exactly one destination per exchange from an expression; recipientList() computes a list of zero, one, or many destinations per exchange from an expression. Reach for toD() when a message goes to exactly one place that varies by message; reach for recipientList() when the same message may need to reach several places at once, and which ones varies by message.

snippets.note: A fixed, always-the-same set of three destinations — every order-confirmed event goes to all three, every time; reading the route shows every destination with nothing left to look up at runtime.

Same three destinations, run concurrently with a bounded total wait, folded into one result by an AggregationStrategy with the identical oldExchange/newExchange shape used by split() and aggregate() in Chapter 13; stopOnException aborts the whole fan-out (instead of silently continuing) the moment any one destination throws.

The destination list is computed per order (which warehouses stock any of its line items) rather than fixed in the route; ignoreInvalidEndpoints() skips a warehouse queue name that doesn't resolve instead of failing the whole order.

A re-configured delimiter (for values that may legitimately contain commas) and an explicit cacheSize bounding how many distinct warehouse-queue producers stay warm in the ProducerCache — the same high-cardinality caution toD()'s cacheSize raised in Chapter 12, here applied to a whole computed list instead of one computed destination.

pitfalls: Writing multicast()/recipientList() with no AggregationStrategy and expecting a combined result downstream — you get the last destination's reply and nothing else, with every earlier destination's result (and any exception it raised) silently gone, the exact failure shape Chapter 13 warned about for split().

Assuming parallelProcessing() lets the route continue past the multicast/recipientList block before every destination finishes — it changes how the destinations run, not whether the calling thread waits for all of them.

Reaching for recipientList() when the destination set is actually always the same — that trades multicast()'s "read the route, see every destination" clarity for a runtime lookup with nothing to show for it.

Leaving cacheSize at its default on a recipient list that can compute a very high-cardinality destination set (e.g., a per-customer queue name) — the ProducerCache can thrash, the same caution the Content-Based Routing chapter raised for a high-cardinality toD() expression.

Assuming stopOnException() is the default — it isn't; left unset, a failing destination doesn't stop its siblings, so a partial failure can go unnoticed unless the AggregationStrategy is written to actually check each branch's exchange.getException().

claims.text: enrich() is Camel's Content Enricher: it calls a Producer on a resource endpoint (a request-reply / in-out call, e.g. HTTP or a bean), sending the current exchange to that endpoint to fetch additional data, then combines the result with the original exchange via an AggregationStrategy.

For enrich(), AggregationStrategy.aggregate(Exchange oldExchange, Exchange newExchange) is called with oldExchange as the original exchange (the one flowing through the route before enrich()) and newExchange as the resource exchange (the reply from the enrichment endpoint). The resource exchange is always created as an in-out exchange internally, regardless of the original exchange's pattern.

If enrich() is given no explicit AggregationStrategy, Camel's default behavior is to just use the body obtained from the resource endpoint as the outgoing message body — the resource's reply silently replaces whatever was there before, discarding the original body.

enrich() supports a dynamic resource URI computed from an expression evaluated against the current exchange, e.g. .enrich().simple("http:myserver/${header.orderId}/order"), so the enrichment source can vary per message.

pollEnrich() is Camel's other Content Enricher variant: instead of a Producer, it uses a Polling Consumer to pull data from the resource endpoint (e.g. read a file, poll an FTP directory, take the next message off a seda/JMS queue) rather than sending the original exchange to it. It does not push any data from the current exchange to the resource endpoint by default — it only reads from a fixed (or dynamically computed) endpoint URI.

pollEnrich()'s timeout argument controls its Polling Consumer semantics: a negative value (the default, -1) waits until a message is available and can block indefinitely (maps to the consumer's receive() method); 0 attempts to receive immediately and returns null if nothing is available (receiveNoWait()); a positive value waits up to that many milliseconds and returns null if it times out (receive(timeout)). Camel's own documentation calls it 'good practice' to always supply an explicit timeout rather than rely on the indefinite-block default.

For pollEnrich(), the same AggregationStrategy.aggregate(oldExchange, newExchange) shape applies, with oldExchange the current/original exchange and newExchange the polled resource exchange — and if the poll finds no data available within the timeout, newExchange is null, so a supplied strategy must handle a null newExchange explicitly.

Both enrich() and pollEnrich() share an aggregateOnException option (default false): when false, if the call to the resource endpoint throws, the AggregationStrategy is skipped entirely and the exception propagates as-is; setting it true routes the failure into aggregate() instead, letting the strategy decide what to do with a failed enrichment.

Both enrich() and pollEnrich() cache producers/consumers for dynamic (expression-computed) resource URIs via a cacheSize option (default 1000). Camel's guidance: if every dynamically computed endpoint is essentially unique, turn caching off by setting cacheSize to a negative value, since caching a large number of one-off endpoints just leaks memory; caching helps when a bounded, reused set of dynamic endpoints repeats across messages.

Because enrich() and pollEnrich() make a synchronous, blocking call to the resource endpoint on the calling thread, a slow or unavailable external system used for enrichment can stall the whole route. Camel's documented mitigation is the same one used for any blocking outbound call: wrap the call in the Circuit Breaker EIP (camel-resilience4j) — e.g. .circuitBreaker().to("http://fooservice.com/faulty").onFallback().transform().constant("fallback").end() — so a failing or slow enrichment source trips open and falls back instead of hanging every exchange that needs enrichment.

The Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j) EIP's key tunables include failureRateThreshold, waitDurationInOpenState, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState, slidingWindowSize, minimumNumberOfCalls, and timeoutDuration — giving an enrichment call an explicit cap on how long it's allowed to hang before the breaker treats it as a failure.

The Content Enricher is originally a Hohpe & Woolf Enterprise Integration Pattern: a specialized transformer that accesses an external data source (a computation, a database, a file, a directory, another system, or even manual entry) to append missing information to a message using data already present in it, such as a key field used to look the rest up.

pollEnrich() does not automatically forward data from the current exchange into the poll (e.g. it can't implicitly reuse an upstream Exchange.FILE_NAME header to pick which file to read) — the endpoint URI must either be static or built from an expression that explicitly pulls what it needs from the current exchange, the same dynamic-URI mechanism enrich() uses.

snippets.note: enrich() calling a producer endpoint with an explicit AggregationStrategy; oldExchange = original order exchange, newExchange = the customer-lookup reply
pollEnrich() with an explicit 10-second timeout, per Camel's 'always set a timeout' guidance
Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j) EIP wrapping a blocking outbound call, the documented pattern for protecting a route from a slow/unavailable enrichment source

pitfalls: Leaving enrich() with no AggregationStrategy silently discards the entire original message body, keeping only the resource's reply — the same class of quiet-default trap as split()/multicast() defaulting to 'last result wins'.

Leaving pollEnrich()'s timeout at its default (-1) means it can block the calling thread indefinitely waiting for data to appear on the resource endpoint; Camel's own docs call an explicit timeout 'good practice'.
A custom AggregationStrategy for pollEnrich() that doesn't check for a null newExchange will throw a NullPointerException the first time the poll times out with nothing available.

aggregateOnException defaults to false, so by default a failed enrichment call skips the AggregationStrategy entirely and the exception just propagates — easy to assume (wrongly) that the strategy gets a chance to supply a fallback value.

Setting cacheSize too high (or leaving the 1000 default) for a dynamic resource URI built from something high-cardinality (e.g. a per-customer or per-order URI) leaks producers/consumers; setting it too low (or negative) for a small, reused, bounded set of dynamic URIs throws away caching that would have helped.

Because enrich()/pollEnrich() block the calling thread on the external call, an enrichment source with no timeout and no circuit breaker turns one slow downstream dependency into an outage for every route that enriches through it.

claims.text: Messaging systems in practice offer at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once: a producer or consumer that retries after a timeout, a crash, or a redelivery has no way to know whether the first attempt actually succeeded, so the safe default is to resend. That single design fact is why duplicates are a normal, expected condition in any integration that retries anything, not an edge case.

The Idempotent Consumer pattern (Hohpe & Woolf) filters duplicates at the receiving end instead of trying to prevent them at the source: it computes a unique key for each incoming message, checks that key against a repository of keys already seen, and only lets a message through the first time its key appears.

Camel's idempotentConsumer() EIP takes two things: an Expression that computes the message's unique key (often a header the sender guarantees is stable, e.g. an order ID or a message UUID) and an IdempotentRepository that stores which keys have already been processed.

idempotentConsumer() has three options that decide its exact behavior around in-flight and failed exchanges. eager (default true) adds the key to the repository before the exchange finishes processing, so two copies of the same message arriving concurrently are both caught, not just sequential duplicates. skipDuplicate (default true) automatically filters a duplicate out of the route; setting it false lets the duplicate continue through the route with the boolean exchange property Exchange.DUPLICATE_MESSAGE set, so the route can decide what to do with it (e.g. route it to a dead-letter-style destination instead of silently dropping it). removeOnFailure (default true) removes the key again if the exchange ultimately fails, specifically so a legitimately failed message is still eligible for a genuine retry rather than being permanently treated as a duplicate.

IdempotentRepository is a pluggable SPI (org.apache.camel.spi.IdempotentRepository); Camel ships several implementations with very different durability and topology tradeoffs. MemoryIdempotentRepository is a bounded, LRU in-process map — fastest, but its history is lost on restart and it is not shared across multiple running instances of the same route, so it only truly prevents duplicates in a single-instance, single-run scenario. Durable, shareable options include a JDBC-backed JdbcMessageIdRepository, a Kafka-backed KafkaIdempotentRepository, and cluster-cache-backed repositories over Hazelcast and Infinispan; a Caffeine-backed repository offers a bounded, evicting in-memory cache with more control than the plain memory one.

A running route with more than one process/instance consuming the same source (competing consumers, multiple pods) needs a repository every instance can see — an in-memory repository lets one instance re-process a message another instance already handled, because neither knows what the other has seen.

The Resequencer pattern (Hohpe & Woolf) restores the original order of a sequence of related messages that arrived out of order — a common side effect of parallel processing, retried deliveries, multiple partitions/consumers, or any path where messages for the same logical stream can race each other.

Camel's resequence() EIP takes an expression that extracts each message's sequence value (a timestamp, or an explicit incrementing sequence number/header) and supports two distinct algorithms selected by calling .batch() or .stream() after it, batch being the default if neither is specified.

Batch resequencing (the default) buffers incoming messages into a batch, sorts the whole batch by the sequence expression, and releases it downstream once the batch reaches batchSize (default 100) or batchTimeout elapses (default 1000ms), whichever comes first. It only guarantees order within a batch — a message that is sorted into batch N cannot be reordered relative to a message that already shipped out in batch N-1, so a very late straggler is not corrected, only ever ordered against whatever else was buffered alongside it.

Stream resequencing does not batch at all — it holds a rolling window of up to `capacity` messages, releases each one in order as soon as it is next in the expected sequence, and uses `timeout` to give up waiting on a gap and release what it has. `rejectOld` (default false) can be set to drop/reject any message whose sequence number arrives lower than one already delivered, and `allowDuplicates` (batch mode) controls whether two messages sharing the same sequence value both survive into the sorted batch or the later one silently replaces the earlier one.

The resequencer works only on the set of messages that actually pass through it: if the sequence field is missing, non-comparable, or the upstream did not guarantee it arrives eventually, the resequencer cannot invent order it was never given.

The Throttler pattern controls the rate at which messages flow to a downstream endpoint, protecting a system that cannot handle unlimited concurrent load or that is bound by an external rate limit/SLA.

Camel's throttle(n) EIP allows at most n messages through per time window; the window length is set with timePeriodMillis (default 1000ms), so throttle(3).timePeriodMillis(10000) allows at most 3 messages through in any 10-second window.

By default throttle() blocks the calling thread until it is that message's turn (synchronous delaying). Setting asyncDelayed(true) instead schedules the delayed continuation on a separate thread pool, freeing the calling thread to go on to service other exchanges rather than sitting idle waiting out the throttle window.

throttle() accepts a correlationExpression so the rate limit is applied per key instead of globally — e.g. throttle(5).correlationExpression(header("tenantId")) enforces the 5-per-window cap independently for each distinct tenant, rather than one shared budget across every tenant.

rejectExecution(true) makes an over-limit exchange fail immediately with a ThrottlerRejectedExecutionException instead of queueing/delaying it — a fail-fast choice for a caller that would rather get a fast error than wait.

Idempotent Consumer, Resequencer, and Throttler are complementary, not competing: they each defend against a different failure mode that at-least-once, asynchronous, parallel delivery introduces — duplicate arrival, out-of-order arrival, and bursty/overloading arrival, respectively — and a production route commonly needs more than one of them at once (e.g. a resequencer to restore order, then an idempotent consumer to catch the duplicates a retried delivery introduced).

snippets.note: The simplest idempotentConsumer() shape: an expression (a stable order-id header) plus a bounded in-memory repository. eager/skipDuplicate/removeOnFailure all keep their defaults (true/true/true).

skipDuplicate(false) lets a detected duplicate continue through the route (instead of being silently filtered) so it can be routed somewhere visible via the Exchange.DUPLICATE_MESSAGE exchange property, rather than disappearing without a trace.
Batch resequencing: buffer up to 200 messages (or wait at most 2s), sort by seqnum, release the sorted batch. Defaults are batchSize=100, batchTimeout=1000ms.
Stream resequencing: hold up to 5000 in-flight messages, release each as soon as it is next-in-sequence, give up waiting on a gap after 4s. Does not wait for a full batch before releasing anything.
At most 5 messages per second per tenant, delayed asynchronously so the calling thread isn't blocked waiting out the window.

pitfalls: Assuming a message broker or 'reliable' transport already guarantees exactly-once delivery — nearly all real systems are at-least-once, so any route with retries, redelivery, or multiple consumer instances must expect and handle duplicates itself.

Choosing an idempotency key that isn't actually stable or unique per logical message (e.g. a hash of arrival timestamp, or a header the sender doesn't guarantee) — the Idempotent Consumer can only be as correct as the key it's given.

Using MemoryIdempotentRepository (or leaving the repository choice as an afterthought) in a route that runs as more than one instance or that must survive a restart — an in-memory repository's history doesn't exist anywhere another instance, or a fresh process, can see.

Turning off skipDuplicate without also handling Exchange.DUPLICATE_MESSAGE — a duplicate that isn't filtered and isn't explicitly checked for just gets processed a second time, exactly the outcome the pattern exists to prevent.

Expecting batch resequencing to produce fully guaranteed order end-to-end — it only sorts within one batch; a message arriving after its batch has already shipped is never retroactively reordered against it.

Leaving the resequencer's stream timeout unset or too high when a message that would fill a sequence gap might never arrive — the resequencer then holds every later message hostage waiting for one that isn't coming, instead of releasing what it has.

Applying a single global throttle() where the real constraint is per-downstream-partner (e.g. a shared SLA per external tenant, not per route) — without correlationExpression, one noisy tenant consumes the entire shared budget and starves the others.

Choosing synchronous throttle() (the default) on a route with real concurrency needs — the calling thread blocks for the full delay, which can quietly turn a rate limiter into a de facto concurrency limiter on threads that had other work to do.

claims.text: The SEDA component gives asynchronous, in-VM behavior: messages sent to a seda: endpoint are placed on a BlockingQueue and consumed by a separate thread from the producer's. SEDA queues are only visible within the same CamelContext (a single JVM) and are not persisted — if the JVM terminates with messages still queued, those messages are lost; Camel's own docs recommend JMS for persistence, reliability, or distribution across processes.

seda: defaults to one consumer thread (concurrentConsumers=1) and a bounded LinkedBlockingQueue with a default capacity of 1000 (size=1000), not an unbounded queue — a common outdated assumption. limitConcurrentConsumers (default true) caps concurrentConsumers at 500 and throws if configured higher.

By default (blockWhenFull=false, discardWhenFull=false) a producer sending to a full SEDA queue gets an immediate IllegalStateException ("queue full") rather than blocking or silently dropping. Setting blockWhenFull=true makes the producer thread block until space frees up (optionally bounded by offerTimeout); setting discardWhenFull=true makes the send fail silently — the message is dropped with no exception raised to the caller. The two options are mutually exclusive; enabling both throws IllegalArgumentException at configuration time.

waitForTaskToComplete controls how long a SEDA producer's calling thread waits after enqueueing: Never returns immediately without waiting for the consumer at all; Always waits for the consumer to finish regardless of exchange pattern; IfReplyExpected (the default) waits only when the exchange is request-reply (InOut) and returns immediately for a one-way (InOnly) exchange.

timeout (default 30000ms) bounds how long a SEDA producer will wait when it is waiting at all (per waitForTaskToComplete). If the timeout elapses before the queued exchange is processed, Camel sets an ExchangeTimedOutException on the original exchange and removes the still-queued, unconsumed copy from the queue — the consumer never gets to process a message its producer has already given up on.

multipleConsumers (default false) turns a SEDA queue from point-to-point (one message consumed once) into publish-subscribe: when enabled, every consumer registered on that seda: endpoint receives its own copy of each message instead of the consumers competing for a single delivery.

purgeWhenStopping (default false) discards whatever is still sitting in a SEDA queue when its consumer/route stops, so the route can stop faster — with the tradeoff that anything still queued at shutdown is lost rather than drained.

A SEDA producer never hands the consumer thread the exact same Exchange object it holds: it builds a correlated copy (a distinct Exchange instance, not sharing the original's UnitOfWork) and puts that copy on the queue. For a wait case (Always, or IfReplyExpected on an InOut exchange), once the consumer finishes, Camel copies the results back onto the original exchange, rather than the producer and consumer ever mutating one shared Exchange concurrently.

Camel's own documentation frames direct: and seda: as opposites on exactly this axis: direct: is described as synchronous, invoking the consumer directly with no threading, while seda: is described as asynchronous, exchanging messages on a BlockingQueue with the consumer invoked on a separate thread. Structurally, a direct: producer calls straight into the consumer's processor in the same method call — no queue and no thread hand-off are involved at all, which is why a slow direct: consumer route stalls its caller.

direct:'s own producer options mirror the synchronous, in-process model: block (default true) makes a producer wait for a consumer to become active if none is running yet, bounded by timeout (default 30000ms); failIfNoConsumers (default true) throws a DirectConsumerNotAvailableException when there's no active consumer and block doesn't resolve it.

Wire Tap always copies the original Exchange and forces the copy's exchange pattern to InOnly — fire-and-forget — regardless of what exchange pattern the main route is using, then sends that copy on a separate thread so it runs in parallel with the primary route rather than delaying it.

Wire Tap's copy is shallow by default: it copies the Exchange but does not deep-clone the message body or headers, so the tapped copy and the original can share the same underlying mutable objects. An onPrepare processor can be supplied to deep-clone the copy before it's sent, for cases where the tapped route or the primary route might mutate shared state.

Wire Tap dispatches the tapped exchange through a thread pool (configurable via executorService/executorServiceRef); by default it falls back to Camel's default async thread pool profile (poolSize 10, maxPoolSize 20, maxQueueSize 1000, keepAliveTime 60s, rejected-execution policy CallerRuns). Because the rejection policy is CallerRuns, once that pool and its queue are both saturated, further wire-tapped exchanges are executed synchronously on the calling thread instead of asynchronously — an "async" wire tap can quietly become a blocking call under load unless a dedicated executor service is configured.

Because Wire Tap is fire-and-forget, a failure while processing the tapped copy is recorded on the tapped exchange, not the original — the primary route has no visibility into a tap that failed unless the tapped route is given its own error handling (its own onException or dead-letter destination).

Camel exposes exactly two message exchange patterns (MEPs) as the org.apache.camel.ExchangePattern enum: InOnly, the one-way Event Message pattern (fire-and-forget, no reply expected or produced), and InOut, the Request Reply pattern (the caller waits for a reply that's populated back onto the exchange).

The exchange pattern can be forced in the Java DSL with .setExchangePattern(ExchangePattern.InOnly|InOut), which takes effect from that point in the route onward and can be changed more than once in the same route. On an endpoint URI, exchangePattern=InOnly|InOut is documented as valid only on a consumer endpoint (inside from(...)) — setting it on a producer's to(...) URI is not the supported way to change producer-side wait behavior; use .setExchangePattern() or the two-argument .to(ExchangePattern, uri) form instead.

Camel's base Endpoint default is InOnly, but many components override it based on what the underlying protocol naturally supports: JMS, File, and SEDA all default to InOnly. JMS specifically auto-detects request-reply per message by the presence of a JMSReplyTo header on the incoming message — if it's present the JMS consumer treats the exchange as InOut and the JMS producer honors InOut by creating a temporary reply queue, setting JMSReplyTo and a JMSCorrelationID on the request, and correlating the reply back using that JMSCorrelationID.

Hohpe & Woolf's Request-Reply pattern names the same tradeoff Camel's InOut represents: a synchronous implementation has a single thread block as a polling consumer waiting for the reply, which is simple but ties up a thread and a caller for the whole round trip; an asynchronous implementation lets many outstanding requests share one reply channel and a separate reply-processing thread, trading that simplicity for the added complexity of a callback mechanism that restores the right caller context once a reply eventually arrives.

Hohpe & Woolf's Event-Driven Consumer — the shape Camel's InOnly/event-driven routes implement — is a consumer that is automatically handed each message as it's delivered on its channel, rather than a consumer that has to actively poll or block waiting for one; the messaging system invokes the consumer's callback as messages arrive.

snippets.note: Producer enqueues onto seda:notifyWarehouse and, under the default waitForTaskToComplete=IfReplyExpected on an InOnly exchange, returns immediately; five consumer threads pull from the queue independently.

Forces the producer to wait up to 5000ms for the queued exchange to finish even though it may be one-way; on timeout Camel sets an ExchangeTimedOutException and removes the unconsumed copy from the queue.
A dedicated executorService avoids the default pool's CallerRuns fallback under load; onPrepare deep-clones the copy since Wire Tap's default copy is shallow.

Forcing InOut on a single step so the route waits for a reply even though the consuming endpoint (JMS) defaults to InOnly — the same pattern already introduced in Chapter 8's Understanding the Exchange.

pitfalls: Treating SEDA as unbounded: the default queue capacity is 1000, and the default overflow behavior is to throw immediately, not to grow forever or to silently drop — a producer that doesn't handle that exception (or configure blockWhenFull/discardWhenFull deliberately) will see route failures under a burst it assumed the queue would absorb.

Setting waitForTaskToComplete=Always together with blockWhenFull=true on the same SEDA producer defeats the point of decoupling: the caller can block twice over, once to get onto the queue and again waiting for the consumer to finish.
discardWhenFull=true silently drops the message with no exception raised to the caller — easy to mistake for reliable delivery until a load spike quietly loses messages.

SEDA has no persistence: purgeWhenStopping is false by default, but even when true, queued messages are discarded, not drained — a JVM crash or an ordinary redeploy loses whatever was still queued either way. This is the same at-least-once-delivery problem Chapter 16 covered, except SEDA doesn't even guarantee at-least-once across a restart the way a broker would.

A Wire Tap's exceptions are invisible to the primary route: because the tap runs fire-and-forget on its own thread and the original exchange's callback fires before the tapped route finishes, a failure inside the tapped route never surfaces on the original exchange unless the tapped route has its own error handling.

Wire Tap's default thread pool falls back to CallerRuns when exhausted (pool size 20, queue 1000) — under sustained load an "asynchronous" tap silently becomes a blocking call on the primary route's own thread, which reads as unexplained latency rather than an obvious failure.

The exchangePattern=... URI parameter only works on a consumer endpoint (inside from(...)); trying to set it on a to(...) producer URI to control wait behavior doesn't do what it looks like it should — use .setExchangePattern() or the two-argument to(ExchangePattern, uri) form on the producer side instead.

claims.text: The file:, ftp:, and sftp: components all extend the same GenericFileComponent/GenericFileEndpoint base, so the polling-consumer options that matter most — readLock, delete, move, moveFailed, preMove, noop, doneFileName, idempotent, recursive, include/exclude, maxMessagesPerPoll — are identical across all three; only the connection/authentication options (host, port, username, privateKeyFile, ...) are specific to the remote components.

A file consumer is a scheduled poll consumer: it defaults to an initialDelay of 1000ms before the first poll and a delay of 500ms between subsequent polls; recursive defaults to false, so a directory endpoint does not descend into subdirectories unless recursive=true is set; include and exclude take a regex tested against the filename to decide which files a poll even considers.

readLock defaults to none — out of the box, Camel's file consumer does not protect against picking up a file that a writer is still in the middle of producing. The available strategies are none, markerFile (creates and holds a lock on a sibling <name>.camelLock file — a near-atomic create, but not guaranteed safe across a cluster and not supported by every remote server), changed (polls the file's length/modification timestamp twice, readLockCheckInterval apart, and only proceeds once both snapshots match), rename (attempts an exclusive rename as the lock test itself), fileLock (a Java NIO FileLock, local filesystems only), and idempotent (uses an IdempotentRepository as the lock, which is what makes it the one strategy that can coordinate across a cluster if the repository implementation supports that).

readLockTimeout defaults to 10000ms: once a file has been waiting that long for its lock to be acquired, Camel gives up on that poll cycle and reconsiders the file on a later one rather than blocking indefinitely. Documentation guidance is to keep readLockTimeout at least 2x readLockCheckInterval so a 'changed' strategy actually gets more than one comparison window before it times out.

On the producer side, fileExist decides what happens when the target filename is already occupied: Override (the default — overwrite), Append, Fail (throw an exception), Ignore (skip the write silently), Move (move the pre-existing file out of the way first, using the moveExisting expression), and TryRename (only meaningful together with tempFileName — rename straight from the temp name to the final name with no exists-check at all, which is faster on filesystems, and especially FTP servers, where an exists-check is its own round trip). fileExist=Append cannot be combined with tempPrefix/tempFileName.

tempFileName / tempPrefix make the producer write under a temporary name and rename to the real name only once the write finishes — that rename-on-completion is what lets a separate file consumer treat 'a file exists under its final name' as a reliable signal that the file is complete, without needing a readLock of its own on the reading side.

doneFileName is the same idea from the consumer's side: instead of inspecting the data file's own stability, the consumer waits for a separate, named 'done' file to appear before it will process the data file. It supports two dynamic tokens, ${file:name} and ${file:name.noext}, so one doneFileName expression can derive the done-file's name from whichever data file it accompanies.

Post-processing a consumed file is controlled by delete, move, moveFailed, and preMove, and choosing none of them is itself a default, not an omission: if a route sets neither delete=true, move, nor noop=true, Camel's out-of-the-box behavior is to move the processed file into a hidden .camel subdirectory next to the original — the file isn't deleted, it just looks that way until someone knows to check .camel.

SFTP endpoints are addressed as sftp://host:port/directory?options, defaulting to port 22, and layer SSH-specific configuration on top of the same GenericFile option set: username/password for password auth, or privateKeyFile/privateKeyUri (+ privateKeyPassphrase) for key-based auth.

strictHostKeyChecking defaults to 'no' — host-key verification is effectively disabled unless a route sets it explicitly, which is a real man-in-the-middle exposure and not merely a lint warning. useUserKnownHostsFile defaults to true, meaning Camel will silently read the running process's own ~/.ssh/known_hosts unless knownHostsFile (or knownHostsUri) points it at a dedicated, deployment-managed file instead.

streamDownload=true on sftp:/ftp: hands the route body as a live InputStream instead of first downloading the whole file to a local temp file — the large-file-friendly path, since it avoids buffering the entire object before processing starts. It carries a documented hang/deadlock risk when combined with the default stepwise=true directory navigation on files past roughly half a megabyte (tracked as CAMEL-12472/CAMEL-14506); the workarounds recorded in the tracker are disabling stepwise or pairing streamDownload with localWorkDirectory so the stream is backed by a temp file rather than held open against the live SSH channel.

aws2-s3 endpoints are addressed as aws2-s3://bucketName?options, with accessKey/secretKey/region (or a configured default AWS credentials chain) for authentication. The consumer polls a bucket the same scheduled-poll way a file: endpoint polls a directory, but its default is deleteAfterRead=true — the object is deleted from the bucket once the exchange commits (only on commit, not on a rollback) — which is the S3 analogue of file:'s delete option, except on by default instead of opt-in.

autoCreateBucket also defaults to true on aws2-s3 — a route pointed at a misspelled or not-yet-provisioned bucket name will silently create a new, empty bucket rather than fail loudly, which can hide a configuration mistake behind what looks like a working, if empty, integration.

The aws2-s3 producer's streamingUploadMode=true switches to a multipart upload so a large body can be sent without knowing its total size up front, completing once batchSize or batchMessageNumber is reached — conceptually the S3 counterpart of the file producer's tempFileName pattern, except the atomicity boundary is the multipart-complete call rather than a filesystem rename.

snippets.note: readLock=changed is the common default for real filesystems and network mounts where a producer writes without an atomic rename.
Bounding maxMessagesPerPoll keeps one poll cycle from trying to claim an entire backlog directory at once.
strictHostKeyChecking=yes plus an explicit knownHostsFile is the deliberate override of both insecure SFTP defaults.
stepwise=false is the documented mitigation for the streamDownload hang on larger files (CAMEL-12472).

pitfalls: Assuming readLock is on by default the way it probably should be — it's 'none' out of the box on file:, ftp:, and sftp: alike, so a naive route can read a file mid-write unless readLock is set explicitly.

Wondering where consumed files 'went' when neither delete, move, nor noop was configured — they're sitting in a hidden .camel subdirectory next to the source, Camel's default post-processing action, not deleted.

Leaving strictHostKeyChecking at its SFTP default of 'no' in anything beyond a throwaway test — it disables the exact host-key verification that protects against a man-in-the-middle substituting a different server.

Combining streamDownload=true with the default stepwise=true on files past roughly half a megabyte — a known hang (CAMEL-12472/CAMEL-14506), not a tuning nuance; disable stepwise or add localWorkDirectory instead.

Trusting aws2-s3's autoCreateBucket=true and deleteAfterRead=true defaults without reading them first — a typo'd bucket name creates an empty bucket instead of failing, and a consumer route quietly deletes every object it reads unless deleteAfterRead=false is set on purpose.
Reaching for fileExist=Append together with tempFileName/tempPrefix — Camel rejects the combination; pick one write strategy or the other.

claims.text: camel-http is a producer-only component for calling external HTTP services from a route (e.g. .to("http://api.example.com/orders")); it sends requests using Apache HttpClient 5.x under the hood (Camel 4.13+), and the URI's http:// or https:// scheme is stripped before the call is made, so the endpoint's own scheme is what actually goes over the wire.

throwExceptionOnFailure defaults to true: any HTTP response in the 300-399 range (redirection) or 400+ (client/server error) is treated as an operation failure and raised as a HttpOperationFailedException rather than silently returned as a 3xx/4xx/5xx body. Setting throwExceptionOnFailure=false disables this, and the route instead receives whatever status code and body the server actually sent, which the route must then inspect itself (e.g. via the CamelHttpResponseCode header).

HttpOperationFailedException carries getStatusCode(), getStatusText(), getResponseBody(), getResponseHeaders(), getUri(), and (for redirects) getRedirectLocation()/hasRedirectLocation()/isRedirectError() — enough information to build an onException handler that branches on the actual failure without re-parsing anything.

Key camel-http timeout options: connectTimeout (milliseconds to establish the TCP connection), socketTimeout/soTimeout (milliseconds of inactivity allowed once connected, i.e. how long to wait for the next chunk of data), and connectionRequestTimeout (milliseconds to wait for a free connection from the pool). All three exist because a hung external service can fail in more than one place — never connecting, connecting but never responding, or the client's own pool being exhausted — and a route that only sets one of them is only protected against one of those failure modes.

bridgeEndpoint=true is the option for building an HTTP proxy/passthrough route: it stops Camel from appending the incoming request's own path and query string onto the producer's URI a second time, and forces a no-op cookie store (a bridging route is not a normal client session, so cookies should not be captured or replayed). Without it, proxying naively double-appends the path.

The REST DSL (rest() and restConfiguration() in Java DSL) is a facade for defining REST operations (get/post/put/delete/patch, with a URI path template like "/users/{id}") that is itself independent of any specific HTTP server; restConfiguration().component(...) picks which underlying component actually serves the requests (platform-http is Camel 4's default binding for Spring Boot/Quarkus/Camel Main; netty-http, jetty, undertow, and servlet are the alternatives). Each rest() verb is wired to an implementing route the same way any other endpoint is — typically to("direct:operationName") — so the REST DSL only replaces how a request enters a route, not what the route does with it.

platform-http is Camel 4's default HTTP server binding: in Camel Quarkus it runs on Quarkus's own Vert.x server (via quarkus-vertx-http); in Spring Boot / standalone Camel Main it is an embedded Vert.x server supplied by camel-platform-http-main (camel-platform-http-vertx). Either way, a route author writing rest() DSL does not stand up a servlet container by hand — the platform already has one, and platform-http plugs Camel's routes into it.

bindingMode on restConfiguration() (or per-verb) controls automatic request/response marshalling: off (the default — the route sees/returns a raw body, e.g. an InputStream or String, and marshals it itself), auto (bind if a data format can be determined from Content-Type), json, xml, or json_xml. With bindingMode=json plus a verb's type()/outType() (or, in newer Camel, consumes/produces content negotiation), Camel marshals/unmarshals the message body to/from the declared POJO automatically using the same Jackson data format machinery covered for marshal()/unmarshal() elsewhere in the book — bindingMode is that same mechanism, wired in as a REST DSL convenience rather than an explicit marshal() step.

Two ways to build a REST API in Camel: code-first, where rest() DSL routes are the source of truth and camel-openapi-java derives an OpenAPI document from them (enabled via restConfiguration().apiContextPath("/api-doc"), with apiProperty(...) supplying title/version/other metadata; the generated spec covers both JSON and YAML, and a Swagger UI can be served alongside it) — or contract-first, where an existing OpenAPI YAML/JSON file is the source of truth and rest-dsl-openapi loads and parses it at startup, generating one REST endpoint per operation and routing each to direct:<operationId> by naming convention. In contract-first mode Camel validates on startup that a direct:<operationId> route exists for every operation in the spec and fails fast if one is missing, unless missingOperation is set to permit incremental implementation.

The rest-openapi component is the calling-side counterpart: instead of camel-http's raw URI, a producer can be pointed at an operationId defined in an external OpenAPI spec (e.g. .to("rest-openapi:api-spec.yaml#getUserById")), and Camel resolves the concrete host, path, and required parameters from that spec rather than the route author hand-assembling the URL. This is the REST DSL's calling-side mirror of contract-first serving: the OpenAPI document is the single source of truth for both directions.

Timeouts alone only bound how long a single call waits; they don't stop a route from hammering an already-struggling downstream service on every retry. Camel's Circuit Breaker EIP (circuitBreaker() DSL, backed by Resilience4j) sits in front of a call and can short-circuit further attempts once a failure threshold is crossed, giving the downstream service room to recover instead of being retried into the ground — the natural pairing with connectTimeout/socketTimeout rather than a replacement for them.

from("direct:lookupCustomer")
    .setHeader(Exchange.HTTP_METHOD, constant("GET"))
    .to("http://crm.internal.example.com/api/customers/${header.customerId}"
        + "?connectTimeout=3000&socketTimeout=5000&throwExceptionOnFailure=false")
    .choice()
        .when(header(Exchange.HTTP_RESPONSE_CODE).isEqualTo(200))
            .unmarshal().json(JsonLibrary.Jackson, Customer.class)
        .otherwise()
            .log("Customer lookup failed with status ${header.CamelHttpResponseCode}")
            .to("direct:customerLookupFailed")
    .end();

snippets.note: Code-first REST DSL: JSON binding via bindingMode + type()/outType(), OpenAPI spec exposed at /api-doc
Reading the structured fields off HttpOperationFailedException instead of parsing a generic exception message

pitfalls: Setting only one of connectTimeout/socketTimeout and assuming the endpoint is now 'protected' — an external service that accepts the connection and then goes silent mid-response is a socketTimeout problem, not a connectTimeout problem, and vice versa for a service that never accepts the TCP connection at all.

Proxying a request with camel-http but forgetting bridgeEndpoint=true: the incoming request's path/query gets appended a second time onto the producer URI, so the outbound call goes to the wrong path.

Assuming throwExceptionOnFailure's default catches every problem worth catching — it only fires on 3xx/4xx/5xx responses. A connection that never completes (DNS failure, refused connection, timeout) raises a different exception (e.g. a connect/socket timeout exception), not HttpOperationFailedException, so an onException clause scoped only to HttpOperationFailedException misses that whole failure class.

Leaving restConfiguration() unset, or set to a component that isn't on the classpath for the runtime in use (e.g. assuming platform-http on a plain Camel Main app with no camel-platform-http-main dependency) — the REST DSL is only a facade, and it does nothing without a concrete server component actually bound to it.

In contract-first mode, forgetting that Camel validates the OpenAPI spec's operationIds against direct:<operationId> routes at startup — a typo in either the spec or the route id fails the whole application at boot rather than at request time, which is a feature, but only if you know to look at the startup log rather than assume a silently-skipped operation.

claims.text: Camel offers three main components for relational database access, each at a different level of abstraction: sql (Spring JDBC's JdbcTemplate underneath, with named-parameter support), jdbc (the raw JDBC API directly, no Spring dependency, producer-only), and jpa (entity objects through a JPA provider such as Hibernate, so routes exchange @Entity beans instead of rows).

The sql component's endpoint URI carries the SQL text itself, e.g. sql:select * from projects where id = :#id. Because the endpoint URI already uses ? to separate the address from its options, a literal ? placeholder in SQL text is repurposed: Camel uses # for a positional placeholder and :#name (or :#${expression}) for a named one.

Named parameter values are looked up in a fixed order of precedence: first a Simple expression written directly in the placeholder, then the message body if it is a java.util.Map, then message headers, then exchange variables — so a route can bind :#customerId straight from a header with no extra processor step.

A sql select returns List<Map<String,Object>> in the message body by default, one map per row keyed by column name. outputType=SelectOne collapses a single-row result to one object; outputType=StreamList streams rows one at a time instead of materializing the whole result set; outputHeader redirects the result onto a header instead of replacing the body, which matters when the route still needs its original body afterward (e.g. enriching a message rather than replacing it).

A sql update/insert/delete does not return a result body at all — the OUT message body is null, and the affected row count is only available as a header, not the body. Code that expects update rows the way it expects select rows will find an empty body and needs to read the row-count header instead.

Setting batch=true on the sql component changes what the inbound body means: instead of one set of parameters, Camel expects an iterable of parameter-iterables (one inner iterable per statement execution), so a batch insert of many rows is driven by wrapping many parameter lists into one outer collection.

The jdbc component's endpoint URI only names a DataSource bean (jdbc:dataSourceName); the SQL text itself always comes from the message body, never the URI. It is producer-only — there is no from("jdbc:...") consumer — and it talks to the JDBC driver directly rather than through Spring's JdbcTemplate, so an application that needs Spring-managed transactions around its database calls should reach for the sql (or spring-jdbc) component instead.

jdbc results default to the same shape as sql — an ArrayList of HashMap<String,Object> rows in the body — with useHeadersAsParameters enabling :?name-style substitution from headers, and useGetGeneratedKeys plus a CamelRetrieveGeneratedKeys header exposing auto-generated keys from an insert. Generated-key retrieval and named-parameter substitution are documented as mutually exclusive on this component — combining them is a configuration error, not just a rare edge case.

The jpa component's consumer polls entities of a configured entityClassName and, by default (consumeDelete=true), deletes each entity from the database once it has been handed to the route — so a route that fails downstream after consumption has already lost the record unless consumeDelete is set to false and a status column or lock is used to control what gets re-polled. maximumResults caps how many entities a single poll loads at once, which matters for tables with existing large backlogs — without it, a poll against a huge unprocessed table can try to load the entire result set into memory in one pass.

jpa producers persist or merge whatever entity object(s) are in the message body; sending a java.util.List of entities requires entityType=java.util.List so the component knows to iterate rather than treat the list itself as one entity. For read/bulk operations, query takes a JPQL string directly on the endpoint, namedQuery references a @NamedQuery already declared on the entity class, and nativeQuery runs SQL directly against the database — a nativeQuery without an explicit resultClass returns raw Object[] rows rather than typed entities.

The sql-stored component calls a stored procedure through a template syntax that mirrors a Java method signature, e.g. sql-stored:MY_PROC(INTEGER ${header.num1}, INOUT INTEGER ${header.num2} result1, OUT INTEGER result2) — IN parameters supply a SQL type and a Simple-expression value, OUT and INOUT parameters each name a result; every OUT/INOUT result is written onto a message header named after that declared result name, not onto the body.

The transacted() DSL marks the remainder of the current route as one Spring-managed transaction: under the covers it wraps that remainder in a TransactionTemplate driven by a configured PlatformTransactionManager, and any transactional outbound endpoint invoked from inside that remainder (a sql/jdbc call, a JMS send under a JMS transaction manager) automatically enlists in the already-open transaction rather than opening its own.

Camel supports Spring's propagation behaviors (e.g. PROPAGATION_REQUIRED to join an existing transaction, PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW to always start a fresh one) so a route that calls into a second transacted route can choose whether that second unit of work shares the caller's transaction or commits/rolls back independently of it.

Redelivery inside a transacted() route is handled by the backing transactional resource (the database, or a JMS broker's own redelivery), not by Camel's redeliverPolicy/Dead Letter Channel machinery — that is a materially different retry story than the non-transacted error handling covered elsewhere in the book, and bolting Camel-level redelivery onto a transacted route without accounting for this can double-handle a failure or mask what the resource is already retrying.

Because a Spring transaction context is bound to the calling thread, transacted() only protects work that stays on that thread. Handing an exchange to a different thread mid-route — a seda: endpoint, an async listener — starts execution on the other side outside the original transaction, so transacted() must be the first step after from() and the whole database work must stay on the route's own thread to be covered by one commit/rollback.

camel-sql ships a JdbcMessageIdRepository — the durable, shareable IdempotentRepository implementation named back in the Reliable Message Delivery chapter. Its default table is CAMEL_MESSAGEPROCESSED(processorName, messageId, createdAt); a lookup runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM CAMEL_MESSAGEPROCESSED WHERE processorName = ? AND messageId = ?, and a new key is recorded with INSERT INTO CAMEL_MESSAGEPROCESSED (processorName, messageId, createdAt) VALUES (?, ?, ?). With multiple concurrent consumer instances, the safety of the whole pattern rests on a unique constraint over (processorName, messageId): without it, two instances can both pass the SELECT check before either finishes its INSERT, and both let the same 'new' message through.

camel-sql also ships a JdbcAggregationRepository, the durable counterpart to the in-memory aggregation state used by the Aggregator EIP (Chapter 13) — it persists in-flight aggregated exchanges to a database so an aggregation survives a process restart instead of losing whatever was accumulated in memory. It requires its own Spring PlatformTransactionManager to orchestrate its writes, and can be given a propagation behavior when used inside a route that is already wrapped in transacted().

A DataSource can be wired to these components explicitly with a URI option (sql:...?dataSource=#myDS) or left unset and resolved by Camel's #autowired property binding, which looks up the registry for a single bean matching the required type (javax.sql.DataSource / jakarta equivalent) and uses it if exactly one exists. In a Spring Boot app this means the framework's own auto-configured DataSource bean is normally picked up with no explicit Camel configuration at all.

Spring Boot's JDBC/JPA starters default to HikariCP as the connection pool since Spring Boot 2, tunable via spring.datasource.hikari.* properties such as maximum-pool-size, connection-timeout, idle-timeout, and max-lifetime. Camel does not run its own pool on top — every sql/jdbc/jpa call borrows a connection from whatever DataSource (or EntityManagerFactory) it was handed, so a burst of concurrent routes competing for a small pool is an application-wide sizing problem, not something scoped to one route.
