from("direct:findCustomerOrders")
    .to("sql:select id, status, total from orders where customer_id = :#customerId order by created_at desc?dataSource=#myDS");
snippets.note: Named parameter :#customerId binds from a header; result is List<Map<String,Object>> in the body.
An update's row count is on a header (SqlConstants.SQL_UPDATE_COUNT / CamelSqlUpdateCount), not the body; the body is null after an update.
IN/INOUT/OUT parameters declared method-signature style; OUT/INOUT results land on headers named after the declared result name.
transacted() must be the first step after from(); both sql calls enlist in the same PlatformTransactionManager-backed transaction and commit or roll back together.
Default schema JdbcMessageIdRepository expects; the primary key (or an equivalent unique constraint) is what actually makes concurrent consumers safe, not the SELECT COUNT(*) check alone.

pitfalls: Writing a literal ? placeholder in sql/jdbc SQL text breaks endpoint parsing, because Camel already uses ? to separate the URI from its options — use # (positional) or :#name (named) instead.
Expecting an update/insert/delete's affected-row count in the body: it's null on the body and only available as a header.
jdbc's useGetGeneratedKeys and named-parameter binding are mutually exclusive on that component — combining them is a documented misconfiguration, not just uncommon.

jpa's default consumeDelete=true removes a polled entity from its table immediately, before the rest of the route has necessarily succeeded — a downstream failure after consumption has already lost the record unless consumeDelete=false plus an explicit status/lock strategy is used instead.

Polling a jpa or sql source with no bound on batch size (no maximumResults / no LIMIT) risks loading an entire large backlog into memory on the first poll against a table that already has a lot of unprocessed rows.

transacted() only covers the calling thread: routing into seda: or handing the exchange to another thread mid-route steps outside the transaction, so database work meant to be atomic must stay entirely within the transacted route, with transacted() as its first step.

Assuming Camel's own redeliverPolicy/Dead Letter Channel governs retries inside a transacted() route — redelivery there is the transactional resource's job (the database, or the JMS broker), and layering Camel-level redelivery on top without understanding that can double-handle or mask what's already retrying.

Relying on an idempotent repository's SELECT-then-INSERT check alone under concurrent consumers: without a unique constraint on (processorName, messageId), two instances can both pass the check before either commits its INSERT, and the same 'new' message gets processed twice — the guarantee comes from the constraint, not the check.

claims.text: Camel's core jms component talks JMS 1.1/2.0 to any compliant broker (ActiveMQ Classic, ActiveMQ Artemis, IBM MQ, and others) through Spring's JMS support underneath. camel-activemq is a thin extension of camel-jms pre-configured for ActiveMQ 5.x (its own docs say to see the JMS component for the real documentation); ActiveMQ 6.x uses camel-activemq6, and ActiveMQ Artemis is typically driven through the generic jms component rather than a dedicated one.

A jms endpoint URI names a destination and, optionally, its kind: jms:FOO.BAR and jms:queue:FOO.BAR are equivalent (queue is the default when no prefix is given), while jms:topic:Stocks.Prices requires the topic: prefix explicitly — there is no destination-type default that silently becomes a topic.

A queue is point-to-point: each message is delivered to exactly one consumer, so multiple route instances (or concurrentConsumers threads) consuming the same queue compete for messages and share the load rather than each seeing every message. A topic is publish-subscribe: every active subscriber receives its own copy of each message, and a subscriber that isn't listening at publish time misses it entirely unless it holds a durable subscription (JMS 2.0 needs only durableSubscriptionName; JMS 1.1 additionally needs a clientId that is unique per connection network-wide, which is exactly why ActiveMQ's Virtual Topics exist as a workaround).

connectionFactory is required and has no default; concurrentConsumers sets how many consumer threads a jms consumer runs (default 1), and maxConcurrentConsumers lets that pool grow under load. cacheLevelName controls what Spring's listener container caches across message deliveries (connection, session, consumer) and is auto-selected based on transacted: CACHE_CONSUMER when transacted=false, CACHE_NONE when transacted=true (XA transactions need a fresh session/consumer each time) — for a non-XA local transaction, setting cacheLevelName=CACHE_CONSUMER by hand restores the caching XA gave up.

Two separate knobs govern reliability on the jms component and they are not meant to be combined: acknowledgementModeName (AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE, CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE, DUPS_OK_ACKNOWLEDGE — default AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE) governs plain JMS session acknowledgement, while transacted=true switches the session into a JMS-transacted session that commits or rolls back the whole unit of work at the end of route processing — once transacted=true is set, the acknowledgement mode is no longer the thing deciding delivery outcome.

Producer-side delivery options: deliveryPersistent (default true) sets the JMS PERSISTENT delivery mode so the broker writes the message to disk before acknowledging it; priority (0-9, default 4) and timeToLive (no default — unset means the broker's own default, often unlimited) are ordinary JMS message properties Camel exposes as URI options. On the consumer side, selector takes a JMS selector expression (SQL-92-like syntax over headers/properties) so a route can subscribe to only the messages matching a filter, evaluated by the broker before delivery rather than by Camel after receipt.

Because the JMS spec requires header names to be valid Java identifiers, Camel rewrites header names that use characters JMS doesn't allow before sending — dots become _DOT_ and hyphens become _HYPHEN_ — and reverses the substitution when consuming, so a header like my.custom-header round-trips transparently through JMS even though the wire format never actually saw a dot or a hyphen.

Request-reply (InOut) over JMS defaults to a temporary reply queue: Camel creates one, sets it as the outgoing message's JMSReplyTo, and correlates the eventual reply using JMSCorrelationID — the same JMSReplyTo/JMSCorrelationID mechanism Chapter 17 named when explaining why the jms component defaults its base exchange pattern to InOnly but auto-promotes to InOut whenever a JMSReplyTo is present on the inbound message. Temporary queues are fast and need no extra configuration, but a fixed replyTo destination can be set instead — Camel then filters incoming replies on that shared queue with a JMS selector keyed on JMSCorrelationID, which works in a cluster but is slower than a temporary queue because of the selector evaluation; replyToType=Exclusive skips the selector for a fixed reply queue at the cost of needing a queue name that is genuinely unique to that one endpoint.

requestTimeout (default 20000ms) bounds how long an InOut producer waits for a reply; it can be overridden per-message with the CamelJmsRequestTimeout header. A timed-out request-reply raises an ExchangeTimedOutException on the original exchange, handled the same way as any other exception — structurally the same failure shape Chapter 17 described for a SEDA producer that gives up waiting on its consumer.

A kafka: endpoint URI names one topic (or a comma-separated list, or a regex when topicIsPattern=true): kafka:orders.created. Unlike JMS there is no queue/topic distinction to choose between — every Kafka topic is a partitioned, retained log, and it is the consumer group, not the topic type, that decides whether messages are shared out (competing consumers) or fanned out (each group sees every message).

brokers names the bootstrap server list; groupId identifies the consumer group a Camel Kafka consumer joins. Kafka assigns each partition of a topic to exactly one consumer instance within a group at a time (a rebalance reassigns partitions when instances join or leave), so ordering is only guaranteed within a single partition — two messages on different partitions can be delivered out of relative order even though a single-partition JMS queue naturally preserves the order messages were enqueued in. autoOffsetReset (earliest, latest, none) decides where a brand-new consumer group starts reading when it has no committed offset yet.

autoCommitEnable defaults to true, committing offsets automatically on Kafka's own schedule — simplest, but a failure partway through processing after an offset was already auto-committed means that record is gone from the group's perspective even though the route never finished it. allowManualCommit (with autoCommitEnable=false) exposes a KafkaManualCommit object on the CamelKafkaManualCommit header that a processor calls once it has actually finished handling the record, synchronously or asynchronously via KafkaManualCommitFactory — but the commit must happen on the same thread the consumer polled on, so routing a manual-commit exchange through an async EIP or a different thread risks a ConcurrentModificationException instead of a clean commit.

pollOnError (default ERROR_HANDLER) decides what a Kafka consumer does when polling itself fails: DISCARD drops the batch, RECONNECT tears down and recreates the consumer, RETRY polls again, STOP halts the route, and ERROR_HANDLER routes the failure into Camel's error handling like any other exception. breakOnFirstError (default false), separately, governs what happens when route processing of a specific record fails: with it enabled, the consumer commits the current offset and reconnects so the failing record can be retried on the next poll instead of the whole batch silently marching past it — with auto-commit already in effect for everything before the failure, this still cannot undo records that were auto-committed before the failure occurred.

key or partitionKey on a producer route selects which partition a message lands on (Kafka hashes the key to a partition when no explicit partition is given), which matters because only messages sharing a partition are ordered relative to each other — a route that needs strict per-entity ordering (e.g. every event for one order) should key by that entity's id so all its events land on the same partition.

transacted=true (with transactionalId set) enables Kafka's own producer transactions, atomically committing or aborting a batch of produced records together with RollbackOnly-driven abort semantics. Kafka transactions are not an XA/JTA two-phase-commit participant, though — they cannot be enlisted in the same distributed transaction as a database write the way Chapter 20's Spring PlatformTransactionManager can, so a route that needs an order row and a Kafka event to succeed or fail together as one atomic unit cannot get that guarantee from Kafka transactions alone.

camel-kafka ships a KafkaIdempotentRepository, a third IdempotentRepository implementation alongside Chapter 16's JdbcMessageIdRepository: instead of a table, it publishes processed keys as events to a dedicated Kafka topic and rebuilds its in-memory cache from that topic on startup (finishing after either 30 seconds or an empty poll, whichever comes first), so every instance sharing that topic converges on the same view of what's already been processed without a database in the picture at all.

Only a limited set of value types serialize onto Kafka message headers: String, Integer, Long, Double, Boolean, and byte[]. A header holding any other type is silently skipped rather than raising an error, which is a quiet way to lose a header that worked fine over JMS or in-memory but was never actually of a Kafka-header-safe type.

snippets.note: A queue load-balances across 5 competing consumer threads; a topic fans the same event out to every active subscriber.
InOut over JMS defaults to a temporary reply queue correlated by JMSCorrelationID; requestTimeout bounds the wait and an ExchangeTimedOutException follows a timeout.
Manual commit must run on the consumer's own polling thread; committing after an async EIP or on a different thread risks ConcurrentModificationException.
Keying by orderId sends every event for one order to the same partition, which is what makes those events ordered relative to each other.

pitfalls: Assuming a jms: URI with no prefix is a topic: it's a queue by default; only jms:topic:name opts into publish-subscribe.

Setting both transacted=true and an explicit acknowledgementModeName expecting them to combine: transacted takes over delivery outcome once enabled, and acknowledgementModeName stops being the thing that decides it.

Subscribing to a topic without a durable subscription and expecting messages published while offline to arrive later — a non-durable subscriber only sees messages published while it is actively connected.

Committing a Kafka manual-commit exchange after routing it through an async EIP or a different thread than the one that polled it — the manual-commit contract requires the same thread, and violating it risks a ConcurrentModificationException instead of a clean commit.

Relying on autoCommitEnable's default (true) and assuming a mid-processing failure is safely retried: if the offset auto-committed before the failure, Kafka already considers that record consumed and it will not be redelivered by the broker.

Expecting cross-partition ordering from Kafka the way a single JMS queue naturally preserves enqueue order — Kafka only orders messages within one partition, so unkeyed or badly-keyed events for the same logical entity can land on different partitions and arrive out of order.

Expecting Kafka's transacted=true to participate in the same atomic unit as a database write via Spring's PlatformTransactionManager (Chapter 20) — Kafka transactions are not an XA/JTA two-phase-commit resource.
Putting a non-String/Integer/Long/Double/Boolean/byte[] value on a header expected to survive onto Kafka — unsupported header value types are silently dropped, not rejected with an error.

claims.text: The component catalog is a standalone camel-catalog module (a JSON-schema metadata repository, one record per component/data format/language/EIP) that is the single source of truth generated from annotations in each component's Java source at build time; it is what IDE autocomplete, `camel-maven-plugin` URI validation, and JBang's dependency resolution and dev-mode option suggestions all read from, rather than any of those tools parsing route code by hand.

As of the 4.18.x/Camel-Quarkus 3.27.x catalog there are on the order of 300 components in the catalog (296 listed for Camel Quarkus 3.27.x, with a handful deprecated and roughly 60 flagged JVM-only, meaning they cannot be compiled to a GraalVM native image) — 'search the catalog first' is a real strategy, not a platitude, because most integrations with a named external system already have a purpose-built component.

An endpoint URI has the shape scheme:path?option1=value1&option2=value2. Path segments map to the component's UriPath options (context, positional, e.g. the destination name in jms:queue:orders); query-string segments map to UriParam options and are always separated by &, exactly like a web URL's query string.

Options split into two tiers: component-level options (set once per component instance — credentials, connection URLs, thread-pool sizing — and inherited by every endpoint built from that component) and endpoint-level options (set per URI, and further split into options that only apply when the endpoint is used as a consumer via from(), only as a producer via to(), or both). A component's doc page tables these three groups separately, and that table is the fastest way to check whether a candidate component even supports from() before writing a route around it — camel-http, for instance, is producer-only and has no consumer table at all.

The same option can be set four different ways, in increasing order of how far it is externalized from the route: (1) directly as a URI query parameter; (2) through the type-safe Endpoint DSL / Component DSL in Java, which is the same options compiled instead of string-parsed; (3) through a property placeholder {{key}} embedded in the URI string, resolved from a .properties file, an OS environment variable, a JVM system property, or (in Spring Boot) application.properties/application.yml; or (4) by configuring the component itself in application.properties under camel.component.<scheme>.<option>=value, which Spring Boot's Camel starter auto-configuration wires into the component bean before any route uses it.

A URI option can reference a bean sitting in the Camel Registry with a # prefix — ?connectionFactory=#jmsCF looks up a bean named jmsCF. If the # reference is omitted entirely and the option's declared Java type matches exactly one bean of that type currently in the Registry, Camel autowires it in automatically with no name needed at all; autowiring only works while there is exactly one candidate bean, so a second bean of the same type re-introduces the need for an explicit #beanId or a named-bean qualifier.

A literal value that itself contains characters the URI parser treats as delimiters (&, =, %, a literal # meant as data rather than a registry reference) has to be wrapped as RAW(value) so Camel takes it verbatim instead of trying to split it into more options — the classic case is a password with a & or % in it landing in a query string.

Because & is XML's own reserved character, every URI written inside the XML DSL has to escape it as & (jms:queue:orders?requestTimeout=5000&transacted=true) — a route that works unmodified in the Java or YAML DSL can silently fail to parse once copied into XML if this escaping is missed.

This book's own examples already show the choice this chapter names directly: camel-jms is the generic, spec-level component that speaks to any compliant broker, while camel-activemq is a thin, pre-configured extension of camel-jms whose own documentation just points back at the JMS component for the real reference — the narrower component only earns its place when it removes real configuration burden (broker-specific defaults), not merely because it has the vendor's name on it. The same generic-vs-specific axis reappears in file/ftp/sftp (all extending the same GenericFileEndpoint base, differing only in the connection/auth options) and in sql/jdbc/jpa (three different abstraction levels — rows via Spring's JdbcTemplate, raw JDBC, or JPA entities — over the same relational database).

Camel Quarkus tracks two support-relevant flags per component beyond plain stable/experimental status: deprecated (scheduled for removal — camel-cloud was deprecated in 4.7.0, for example) and JVM-only (works on the JVM runtime but has no GraalVM native-image support), either of which is a real disqualifier depending on the deployment target and worth checking before a component is adopted into a route, not after.

snippets.code:
# application.properties
camel.component.jms.connection-factory = #jmsCF
camel.component.http.connect-timeout = 5000

# the route URI stays short: only the destination and per-endpoint overrides remain
# from("jms:queue:orders.new?concurrentConsumers=5")
snippets.note: component-level defaults set once via Spring Boot auto-configuration instead of repeated on every endpoint URI
RAW() protects a literal value containing URI-delimiter characters (&, %, =) from being parsed as extra options

pitfalls: Wiring a producer-only component (e.g. camel-http) into a from() and only discovering at runtime that it has no consumer — the component's doc page's consumer/producer option tables would have shown this before writing the route.
Forgetting to escape & as & inside the XML DSL, which parses fine in Java/YAML but breaks the XML route on the next option.
Putting a raw password or token containing &, =, or % straight into a URI query string without RAW(), so Camel misparses it into extra bogus options instead of one value.
Registering a second bean of a type Camel was autowiring by type — autowiring silently stops working once there is more than one candidate, and the option needs an explicit #beanId again.

Reaching for a narrow, vendor-named component (e.g. camel-activemq) purely because the vendor's name matches the target system, when the generic component underneath (camel-jms) does the same job with the same options and only the connection details differ.

Adopting a component without checking its deprecated/JVM-only flags in the catalog for the target Camel version and runtime (Quarkus native vs JVM), then discovering the incompatibility at build or deploy time instead of at selection time.

claims.text: Camel's default error handler (DefaultErrorHandler, the built-in default since the 2.x line) is set up automatically even with zero configuration, but it holds no dead-letter destination and does not mark a failed exchange as handled: an exception thrown mid-route and not caught by any onException() clause is logged and then propagated back to the exchange's caller, ending that exchange at the point of failure.

onException(ExceptionType.class, ...) declares a policy for one or more exception classes. When an exception is thrown, Camel's DefaultExceptionPolicyStrategy walks the exception's cause chain from the innermost cause outward and, at each exception in that chain, looks for an onException clause that is an exact instanceof match; failing that, it falls back to the clause whose declared exception is the closest matching superclass. A more specific declared onException (e.g. FileNotFoundException) is preferred over a broader one (e.g. IOException) even both are declared, independent of the order they appear in the route code.

handled(true) on an onException clause tells Camel to swallow the exception once the clause's steps finish running: the exchange is not marked as failed and no exception reaches the original caller. The default, handled(false), logs the failure and still rethrows the exception to the caller. continued(true) goes further than handled(true): it swallows the exception AND resumes the original route from the exact point where the exception was thrown, as though it never happened; handled and continued are alternative endings for the same clause, not settings you combine.

Inside an onException block (or any error handler), the failing exchange's own exchange.getException() call no longer returns the caught exception, because Camel has already moved it onto the exchange as a property. The exception must instead be read with exchange.getProperty(Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT, Exception.class).

onWhen(Predicate) attaches an extra condition to an onException clause on top of the exception-type match: the clause fires only when the thrown exception's type matches AND the predicate evaluates true against the current exchange. This lets two clauses declared for the same exception class handle different situations — for example, treating a SQLException with a known-transient error code differently from one that is not.

doTry().<steps>.doCatch(ExceptionA.class, ExceptionB.class).<steps>.doFinally().<steps>.end() is Camel's DSL equivalent of Java's try/catch/finally, prefixed with "do" to avoid colliding with the Java keywords. It is scoped to just the steps written inside the block, and for the duration of that block the route's own error handler (Dead Letter Channel, DefaultErrorHandler, or any onException policy) is not in effect — doTry...doCatch...doFinally is its own self-contained error handler, not a wrapper around the outer one. doCatch also accepts onWhen() the same way onException does, and the block must be closed with end().

onException() declared at the top level of a RouteBuilder's configure() method — before any from(...) — applies to every route built by that RouteBuilder, which is the classic way to get a single, shared error policy without repeating it on each route. In the Java DSL this global scope is per RouteBuilder instance: it is not automatically shared across separate RouteBuilder classes registered in the same CamelContext unless they extend a common base class that declares the shared onException() clauses.

Route Configurations (routeConfiguration("id").onException(...) / .errorHandler(...)) are the modern, more precise alternative to one context-wide global policy: a named route configuration is defined once and then attached to specific routes via .routeConfigurationId("id"), which accepts exact ids, wildcards, and regular expressions — so different groups of routes can each get their own error-handling policy without copy-pasting onException() into every RouteBuilder.

Business exceptions versus technical exceptions is a design idiom applied on top of Camel's API, not a distinction Camel itself enforces: routes are typically written against a custom exception hierarchy where a business/domain exception (e.g. an OrderValidationException for a malformed or rule-violating order) represents an expected failure that should be handled once, without redelivery, and reported back to the caller or routed to a rejection path — while a technical/infrastructure exception (IOException, SQLException, ConnectException, HttpOperationFailedException) represents an unexpected environment failure that is often transient and worth redelivering and/or dead-lettering. Declaring one onException() clause per category is the common way to express the split in a route.

useOriginalMessage() (or useOriginalBody() for just the body) on an onException or error-handler configuration restores the exchange's message to how it looked when it first entered the route, discarding any transformation that happened before the failure. It depends on Camel's Unit of Work having retained that original message, which carries a memory and performance cost, so it is opt-in rather than the default.

A redelivery policy (maximumRedeliveries, redeliveryDelay, and related backoff options) can be attached to any onException() clause or to the route's top-level error handler, but maximumRedeliveries defaults to 0 — no redelivery happens at all until it is explicitly configured. Tuning these settings and routing exhausted exchanges to a Dead Letter Channel destination is the subject of the next chapter.

A named route configuration attached to one route by id; other routes can opt out or use a different configuration. Verified against the Camel 4.x Route Configuration manual.

pitfalls: Assuming onException() automatically retries a failed exchange — maximumRedeliveries defaults to 0, so without explicit redelivery configuration the clause runs once and either rethrows or swallows, it never resends on its own.
Forgetting handled(true) and being surprised the caller still sees the exception — the default is handled(false), which logs and rethrows.

Calling exchange.getException() inside an onException block and getting null — once inside the block the exception lives on the Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT property, not the exchange's own exception field.

Assuming a doTry block still runs under the route's outer onException policy — it doesn't; doTry defines its own private error handler for that scope only, so an outer onException for the same exception type will not fire inside it.

Declaring onException(Exception.class) as an early catch-all — it matches almost anything, including bugs that should have surfaced loudly, and can silently swallow failures a narrower, more specific clause would have handled differently.
Forgetting the closing end() on a doTry/doCatch/doFinally block in the Java DSL, which leaves the block improperly closed.

claims.text: Redelivery is configured through a RedeliveryPolicy, set via maximumRedeliveries(...), redeliveryDelay(...) and related methods on an onException clause or on errorHandler(...). The default RedeliveryPolicy has maximumRedeliveries=0, which disables redelivery entirely — declaring an onException clause with no redelivery settings gets zero retries, exactly one attempt, unless maximumRedeliveries is set explicitly (a positive number of retries, 0 to disable, or a negative number for unlimited redelivery).

The default fixed redeliveryDelay is 1000ms (1 second) between attempts. Enabling useExponentialBackOff(true) makes each successive delay the previous delay multiplied by backOffMultiplier (default 2.0), so delays grow 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...; maximumRedeliveryDelay caps how large that computed delay is allowed to grow (default 60000ms / 60 seconds), so exponential growth does not run away to hours-long waits.

useCollisionAvoidance(true) adds a small random jitter to each computed delay, which matters most when many exchanges fail at once (e.g. a downstream outage) — without jitter, every failed exchange would retry in lockstep and hit the recovering system with a synchronized burst at the same instant.

delayPattern is an alternative to a fixed/exponential delay: a string like "5:1000;10:5000;20:20000" means attempts 0-4 use 0ms delay, attempts 5-9 use 1000ms, attempts 10-19 use 5000ms, and attempt 20+ uses 20000ms. When delayPattern is set, redeliveryDelay, backOffMultiplier, useExponentialBackOff and useCollisionAvoidance are all ignored — it replaces that whole calculation, it does not compose with it.

asyncDelayedRedelivery(true) schedules the wait for the next redelivery attempt on Camel's redelivery thread pool instead of blocking the current processing thread for the full delay. Without it, a route's caller thread sleeps through every redelivery delay; with it, the thread is freed to do other work and the redelivery is resumed later from a scheduled task.

retriesExhaustedLogLevel controls the log level used for the final failure message once maximumRedeliveries is reached and no more attempts will be made; it defaults to ERROR. A separate retryAttemptedLogLevel (default DEBUG, often raised to INFO/WARN in production) controls the level logged before each individual redelivery attempt — keeping the two separate lets a route stay quiet about routine retries while still logging loudly the moment a message is truly given up on.

onRedelivery(Processor) on a RedeliveryPolicy / error handler runs immediately before each redelivery attempt (not before the first, original attempt), so it can be used to mutate the exchange, add a header recording the attempt, or emit a metric per retry. It is scoped to whichever onException clause or errorHandler declares it, unlike a route-wide interceptor.

Two Dead Letter Channel options shape exactly what gets sent to the dead-letter destination once redeliveries are exhausted: useOriginalMessage() sends the exchange's original incoming message body/headers rather than whatever the route had transformed it into by the point of failure, and deadLetterHandleNewException(false) (default true) controls whether a second exception thrown while moving the exchange to the dead-letter destination itself is caught (so the original failure isn't masked) or allowed to propagate.

Dead Letter Channel is configured either as the route's error handler — errorHandler(deadLetterChannel("jms:queue:dead").maximumRedeliveries(5).redeliveryDelay(5000)) — which applies to every exception not otherwise claimed by a more specific onException clause, or per-exception by pairing onException(...) with a redelivery policy and a .to(deadLetterUri) destination at the end of the clause, which was the pattern used for ConnectException/SQLException in the exception-handling chapter.

Once an exchange's redeliveries are exhausted, Camel marks it with exchange properties recording the outcome — including a redelivery counter and a flag that the exchange is exhausted — readable via Exchange.REDELIVERED / Exchange.REDELIVERY_COUNTER / Exchange.REDELIVERY_MAX_COUNTER properties on the exchange, the same property-based mechanism (rather than a getter) used for Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT in the exception-handling chapter.

With DefaultErrorHandler (no dead-letter destination configured) exhausted redeliveries end the same way an unhandled exception always does: logged and propagated back to the exchange's caller. With Dead Letter Channel, the exhausted exchange is instead moved to the configured dead-letter destination and, unless handled(false) is explicitly set, the exchange is marked handled — the original caller sees a normal completion, not a propagated exception, because the failure has been redirected rather than surfaced.

A durable dead-letter destination (a JMS/ActiveMQ dead-letter queue, a Kafka DLQ topic, a database table, a directory of failed-message files) turns 'redeliveries exhausted' from a lost message into an inspectable, replayable one: operations tooling (e.g. a JMS broker's web console) can move a message from the dead-letter destination back to the original input queue once the root cause is understood and fixed.

Blind, automatic replay of everything in a dead-letter destination is a known anti-pattern: a message that failed because of a bad payload or a code defect (a genuine 'poison message') fails identically on replay and just re-poisons the queue. Replay is safe once the root cause is understood to be transient (the kind of failure redelivery already exists for) or once the underlying bug/data problem has actually been fixed — not as a default recovery action.

Because at-least-once redelivery and dead-letter replay can both cause the same logical message to be processed more than once, a route that redirects failures to a dead-letter destination for later replay should pair it with the Idempotent Consumer pattern (idempotentConsumer(), covered under reliable message delivery) on the reprocessing path — otherwise a replayed order or payment is applied twice.

Redelivery policy is normally reserved for technical exceptions (the environment misbehaving, plausibly transient); business exceptions representing a genuine domain-rule violation are typically handled(true) with maximumRedeliveries left at its default of 0, since retrying a validation failure produces the identical rejection every time and only delays the response.

snippets.note: per-exception redelivery policy with exponential backoff, verified against RedeliveryPolicy option names
route-wide Dead Letter Channel as the error handler
onRedelivery processor reading the redelivery counter property

pitfalls: Declaring onException(SomeException.class) with no maximumRedeliveries set gets zero retries — the default RedeliveryPolicy has maximumRedeliveries=0, so the clause only changes what happens after the (single) failure, not how many times Camel tries first.
Exponential backoff without maximumRedeliveryDelay can produce absurdly long waits on a long-running exhaustion sequence; always set a cap alongside useExponentialBackOff().

Treating the dead-letter destination as a silent trash can instead of an inspectable queue — without monitoring/alerting on it, messages pile up unnoticed until someone asks why an order never shipped.
Blind auto-replay of an entire dead-letter queue re-poisons it: a payload-shape or code-defect failure reproduces identically on replay.

Replaying a dead-lettered message without an idempotent consumer on the reprocessing path can cause the same order/payment to be applied twice if the original attempt had actually partially succeeded downstream before failing.

claims.text: A Processor is a plain Java object with a process(Exchange) method and no dependency on a running CamelContext to be exercised in a test: a unit test can new up the processor directly, build a DefaultExchange (optionally against a lightweight DefaultCamelContext used only to construct the exchange), populate its body/headers, call process(exchange) directly, and assert on the resulting exchange — no route, no context startup, no mock endpoints involved.

camel-test-junit5 is the JUnit 5 testing module; its central class is org.apache.camel.test.junit5.CamelTestSupport, a base class a test extends to get a running CamelContext plus a ProducerTemplate (template) and ConsumerTemplate (consumeTemplate) wired up automatically for the test's lifetime. The test supplies its routes by overriding createRouteBuilder() to return the RouteBuilder under test.

MockEndpoint is Camel's dedicated test-double endpoint, reached via a mock: URI (e.g. mock:results). A route under test is rewired — either by literally routing .to("mock:results") in a test-only route, or via auto-mocking/AdviceWith (see below) — so an assertion can be set on the mock before a message is sent, the message is sent, and the mock is asked to confirm its expectations were met.

The core MockEndpoint assertion methods: expectedMessageCount(int) sets how many exchanges must arrive; expectedBodiesReceived(Object...) sets the expected bodies in order (and, if also set, overrides the count implied by expectedMessageCount to match the number of bodies given); expectedHeaderReceived(String, Object) and expectedPropertyReceived(String, Object) check a specific header/property on every received exchange. All expectations are configured before the exchange is sent, then assertIsSatisfied() is called afterward to verify them.

MockEndpoint.assertIsSatisfied() polls for up to a configurable result-wait-time (10 seconds by default, changed via setResultWaitTime(millis)) before failing, rather than checking instantaneously — which matters for routes with any asynchronous hop (SEDA, a thread pool, a JMS/Kafka consumer) where the expected exchange may not have arrived at the mock the instant send() returns.

whenAnyExchangeReceived(Processor) and the index-specific whenExchangeReceived(int index, Processor) let a mock endpoint script behavior instead of just recording exchanges — including throwing an exception from inside the processor. whenExchangeReceived(0, ex -> { throw ... }) makes the first exchange received fail while later ones succeed, which is the mechanism for testing "fails N times then succeeds" retry scenarios against a mock standing in for a flaky downstream system.

CamelTestSupport can auto-mock endpoints without editing the route under test at all: overriding isMockEndpoints() to return a URI pattern (or "*" for everything) makes Camel insert a mock endpoint in front of every matching endpoint — the message still also goes to the real endpoint. Overriding isMockEndpointsAndSkip() instead does the same interception but skips sending to the real endpoint, so the mock fully substitutes for it — the version to reach for when the real endpoint is an external system a test must not actually call.

AdviceWithRouteBuilder (used via context.adviceWith(routeId, AdviceWithRouteBuilder) or adviceWith(routeId, builder -> {...}) in newer APIs) lets a test rewrite a specific, already-built route for the duration of that test without touching the production RouteBuilder source: weaveByType(NodeType.class) selects nodes by their EIP type (this includes onException clauses, not just route body steps), weaveById(id) selects by a node's declared id, and weaveByToUri(uriPattern) selects .to() endpoints by URI. Each selection is then acted on with .replace(), .remove(), .before(), or .after() to substitute, delete, or splice in new behavior — most often replacing a real endpoint with a mock: or direct: test double.

adviceWith() also exposes two shortcut methods scoped to the advised route: mockEndpoints(pattern) and mockEndpointsAndSkip(pattern), the AdviceWith-scoped equivalents of CamelTestSupport's isMockEndpoints()/isMockEndpointsAndSkip() — useful when only one route in a multi-route test class needs its endpoints mocked, rather than every route the test context loads.

The official guidance is to advise a given route only once per test: calling adviceWith on the same route id a second time is not supported and can produce broken or unpredictable results, especially once an error handler is involved. A test that needs several different weavings of the same route should split them across separate test methods (each getting a freshly built context/route), not chain multiple adviceWith calls against one route instance.

AdviceWith requires the route not to have started yet when the advice is applied, so CamelTestSupport's isUseAdviceWith() must be overridden to return true — this stops the test context from auto-starting the route on setup, giving the test a window to call adviceWith() before starting the context itself.

NotifyBuilder is an alternative to mock endpoints for knowing when a route has finished processing, built from expressions like whenDone(int), whenCompleted(int), and whenFailed(int) and checked with wasSatisfied() (immediate) or matches(timeout, TimeUnit) (polls/waits). It watches the CamelContext's event notifications rather than requiring any .to("mock:...") wiring, which makes it the natural choice for asserting completion of a route a test doesn't want to alter at all — e.g. confirming an async SEDA/Wire Tap hop actually completed, or that a message ultimately failed, without adding a mock endpoint to the route.

whenDone(n) matches once n exchanges have finished being routed regardless of outcome (success or failure both count as "done"); whenCompleted(n) matches only on successful completions; whenFailed(n) matches only on exchanges that ended in failure. This distinction is what makes NotifyBuilder practical for asserting retry-and-give-up scenarios: whenFailed(1) can confirm an exchange that exhausted its redeliveries really did end up marked as failed, independent of how many redelivery attempts happened along the way.

To test redelivery/backoff behavior without a test actually sleeping through real delays, the route's RedeliveryPolicy needs a much smaller redeliveryDelay for the test run — either by parameterizing the delay via a property placeholder that the test overrides (e.g. a lower value in a test-scoped application.properties / useOverridePropertiesWithPropertiesComponent), or by using adviceWith's weaveByType(OnExceptionDefinition.class) to swap in a test-only onException/redelivery policy with a near-zero delay. Either way, the test still exercises the real retry mechanism and counts real attempts — it just doesn't wait through real-world backoff timings to do it.

camel-test-spring-junit5 adds Spring-aware testing support for Camel-on-Spring-Boot applications: @CamelSpringBootTest boots the Spring context together with Camel; @MockEndpoints(pattern) and @MockEndpointsAndSkip(pattern) are class-level annotations that apply the same auto-mock/auto-mock-and-skip behavior CamelTestSupport exposes via method overrides, without needing to extend CamelTestSupport directly; @UseAdviceWith defers route startup the same way isUseAdviceWith() does, so a @Test method can call adviceWith() before the context starts.

camel-quarkus ships its own JUnit 5 testing support (camel-quarkus-junit5) built on Quarkus's @QuarkusTest rather than camel-test-junit5's CamelTestSupport — Quarkus routes are typically tested through the same CDI-managed CamelContext the application boots, with mock endpoints and RestAssured (for REST DSL routes) layered on top, reflecting Quarkus's build-time-wiring model rather than the manually-constructed context camel-test-junit5 assumes.

A practical layering for a route's test suite mirrors the pyramid: fast, dependency-free unit tests calling processors' process(Exchange) directly for pure transformation/validation logic; CamelTestSupport-based route tests using mock endpoints and/or AdviceWith to swap out real systems (files, HTTP, JMS, databases) for test doubles, verifying routing decisions and error handling without touching a real external system; and a smaller number of true integration tests (e.g. with Testcontainers) that exercise a route against a real instance of a downstream system to catch what a mock can't — wire-format mismatches, connection/auth issues, timeouts under real network conditions.

snippets.note: unit-testing a plain Processor with no CamelContext started — no route, no mock, no Camel test base class
CamelTestSupport + a mock endpoint wired into the route under test, asserting body content and count
isMockEndpointsAndSkip() auto-mocks every http: endpoint and skips the real call, scripting the stand-in's response
AdviceWith swaps in a zero-delay redelivery policy so the test proves the retry count without waiting through real backoff; whenExchangeReceived scripts the first two attempts to fail
NotifyBuilder confirms an exchange ended in failure without adding a mock endpoint or altering the route

pitfalls: Calling assertIsSatisfied() before sending any messages, or setting expectations after sending — expectations must be configured on the mock before the message is sent; assertIsSatisfied() is the check that runs afterward.

Forgetting isUseAdviceWith() (or @UseAdviceWith on Spring) before calling adviceWith(): without it the route has already started by the time the test tries to advise it, and the advice either fails or silently doesn't apply.

Calling adviceWith() more than once against the same route id — unsupported, and especially unreliable once an error handler is involved; each distinct weaving belongs in its own test method with a fresh context.

Using isMockEndpoints() when the intent was to prevent a real call: isMockEndpoints() still sends to the real endpoint after mocking it, so a test aimed at an external system will actually hit it unless isMockEndpointsAndSkip() (or AdviceWith's mockEndpointsAndSkip()) is used instead.

Writing a route test that sleeps through real redeliveryDelay/backOffMultiplier timings to prove retry behavior — slow, flaky under CI load, and unnecessary; override the policy (or its delay) to near-zero for the test instead, since what's under test is the retry count and outcome, not real-world timing.

Relying on MockEndpoint's default 10-second result-wait-time for a route with any async hop and assuming a failed assertIsSatisfied() means the message never arrived, when it may simply have arrived after the wait window — widen setResultWaitTime() for routes with real async or slow downstream calls instead of guessing.

Testing every route exclusively through full CamelTestSupport route tests with real (or mocked) endpoints, and never unit-testing processors directly — pure transformation/validation logic in a Processor is faster and more precisely tested with a bare process(exchange) call than by routing a message through an entire Camel context to reach it.

claims.text: The log() Log EIP takes an SLF4J-style message template with Simple-language placeholders (e.g. log("Processing order ${header.orderId}")) and an optional LoggingLevel and logName, and is the recommended way to write steady-state production log lines from a route. The separate log: component endpoint (to("log:orderRoute?showAll=true")) is a debugging/troubleshooting tool: showAll=true dumps the entire exchange (all headers, properties, and body) on every message, which is useful while developing a route but too noisy and too revealing to leave running in production.

logMask (camel.main.logMask=true, or context.setLogMask(true) in Java) turns on automatic masking of over five dozen well-known sensitive keywords (password, apiKey, token, secret, and similar) wherever the Log EIP or log: component would otherwise print a header or property value verbatim; camel.main.additionalSensitiveKeywords extends the built-in list with application-specific keywords.

Camel stamps a breadcrumbId header on every exchange when useBreadcrumb is enabled, which is the default; the value falls back to the exchange's own messageId when no breadcrumbId already exists on an inbound message. Because it lives in a header rather than internal exchange state, it survives any transport that preserves headers (HTTP, JMS, and similar), so the same breadcrumbId can be grepped across every service a message passes through end to end.

Exchange.CORRELATION_ID is a distinct, Camel-internal exchange property (not the breadcrumbId header) that Camel sets on a sub-exchange spun off by certain EIPs to link it back to the exchange it was derived from; a route can also define its own application-level correlation id by setting an ordinary header and reading it back later in the flow.

Legacy MDC logging is enabled with camel.main.useMdcLogging=true (application properties) or context.setUseMDCLogging(true) (Java), and populates SLF4J's MDC with camel.breadcrumbId, camel.exchangeId, camel.messageId, camel.correlationId, camel.routeId, camel.stepId, camel.contextId, and camel.transactionKey for the duration of processing, so a log pattern referencing e.g. %X{camel.exchangeId} ties every log line touched by one exchange together without changing a single log() call. This approach is deprecated as of Camel 4.19 in favor of the camel-mdc component.

The camel-mdc component (the replacement for legacy MDC logging) is enabled with camel.mdc.enabled=true and promotes chosen exchange headers or properties into MDC declaratively via camel.mdc.customHeaders / camel.mdc.customProperties, rather than requiring a processor to call org.slf4j.MDC.put by hand; the two approaches must not be enabled at the same time.

MDC context set on one thread does not automatically follow an exchange onto Camel's own async worker threads (SEDA queues, thread pools, and other hand-offs), so a naive MDC.put in a processor can silently go missing exactly at a route boundary where the thread changes; the camel-mdc component's exchange-header-driven approach avoids this because the value travels with the exchange itself instead of living on a thread-local.

MicrometerRoutePolicyFactory auto-instruments every route in a CamelContext with counters and timers with no per-route code: camel.exchanges.total, camel.exchanges.succeeded, camel.exchanges.failed, camel.exchanges.failures.handled, and camel.exchanges.external.redeliveries as counters, plus a camel.route.policy timer capturing exchange duration per route. Camel 3.21 and later use Micrometer's dotted naming convention (camel.exchanges.total); 3.20 and earlier used camelCase names like CamelExchangesTotal.

MicrometerRoutePolicyFactory is not wired up automatically just by adding camel-micrometer(-starter) to the classpath; it must be registered explicitly, either with camelContext.addRoutePolicyFactory(new MicrometerRoutePolicyFactory()) in Java or by exposing it as a Spring bean in a Spring Boot application. Spring Boot's autoconfiguration does automatically wire Camel's metrics into whatever MeterRegistry bean is on the classpath (e.g. from spring-boot-starter-actuator), so the counters end up on the same /actuator/prometheus endpoint as the JVM and HTTP metrics with no separate registry to configure.

The micrometer:counter and micrometer:timer endpoints let a route push its own business-level metrics inline, separate from the automatic route-policy metrics: to("micrometer:counter:orders.processed") increments a counter by 1 by default (or by an increment/decrement URI option or CamelMetricsCounterIncrement/CamelMetricsCounterDecrement header), and a micrometer:timer pair with action=start before a block of steps and action=stop after it measures that block's elapsed time as a single named Micrometer timer.

camel-opentelemetry creates spans for messages sent to and from Camel and is added to a Spring Boot app via the camel-opentelemetry-starter dependency, configured either through the OpenTelemetry Java agent or through Spring Boot Actuator plus micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel; incoming trace context arrives on the standard W3C traceparent header, which Camel exposes to a route as an ordinary exchange header. This component is deprecated as of Camel 4.19.0 in favor of camel-opentelemetry2, the newer, recommended component for tracing new Camel applications.

When OpenTelemetry instrumentation and MDC logging are both active, OpenTelemetry's own logger auto-instrumentation adds trace_id and span_id into the same MDC map Camel populates, so a single log line can be filtered by both a Camel-native identifier (camel.exchangeId, camel.routeId) and a distributed trace identifier (trace_id) at once, tying a log line to both the local exchange and the cross-service trace it belongs to.

camel-health auto-registers a context health check (is the CamelContext started), a routes check (are all discovered routes started), a consumers check (per-consumer input checks), and a registry check (any custom HealthCheck beans found in the registry) as soon as camel-health is on the classpath; producer checks are opt-in via camel.health.producersEnabled=true, and each category can be toggled independently with camel.health.routesEnabled, camel.health.consumersEnabled, and camel.health.registryEnabled.

A HealthCheck is, by default, usable as both a readiness and a liveness check; a custom check overrides isReadiness() (and/or isLiveness()) to restrict itself to one or the other. Spring Boot exposes the aggregated result at /actuator/health (folding Camel's checks into Spring's own health groups); Quarkus exposes the equivalent at /q/health, split into /q/health/ready and /q/health/live.

snippets.note: Log EIP with a Simple-language message template; distinct from the log: component used for exchange-dumping debug output.
The current (camel-mdc) way to enable MDC: promote named exchange headers into SLF4J MDC declaratively, without a legacy useMDCLogging + manual MDC.put mix.
Registering the route-policy metrics factory as a Spring bean so every route gets camel.exchanges.* counters and a camel.route.policy timer with no per-route code.
A custom readiness-only health check: a downstream outage should take the pod out of the load balancer's rotation, not trigger a container restart.

pitfalls: Enabling legacy useMDCLogging and the newer camel-mdc component at the same time is explicitly unsupported — pick one, and on Camel 4.19+ prefer camel-mdc.

MDC values set by hand with org.slf4j.MDC.put in a processor don't automatically survive a hop onto Camel's own async worker threads (SEDA, thread pools) — the context can silently go missing exactly at a route boundary, which is the moment it's needed most.

to("log:name?showAll=true") is a development/debugging tool, not a production logging strategy: it dumps the full exchange (every header, property, and the body) on every message, which is both noisy and, without logMask also enabled, a sensitive-data leak risk.
camel-opentelemetry is deprecated as of Camel 4.19 in favor of camel-opentelemetry2; a project pinned to the 4.18 LTS line can still use it, but new tracing work should reach for the v2 component.

Treating a downstream dependency outage as a liveness failure instead of a readiness failure causes a container orchestrator to restart a perfectly healthy process that can't fix a problem that isn't its own — failing readiness alone lets Kubernetes simply stop sending it traffic until the check recovers on its own.

claims.text: A property placeholder in Camel uses the syntax {{key}}; {{key:default}} supplies a fallback value used only when the key can't be resolved; {{?key}} makes the whole option optional, so an endpoint keeps its own built-in default and the route doesn't fail to start when the key is absent, rather than substituting a placeholder-level default value; and prefixing the key with ! negates a boolean result, e.g. {{!integration.ftpEnabled}}.

Placeholders can nest: a resolved value can itself contain another {{...}} reference (e.g. cool.concat=mock:{{cool.foo}}), which Camel resolves recursively. Nesting is on by default and can be turned off per-lookup with the nested=false option (e.g. {{myQuery?nested=false}}) for values such as JSON that legitimately contain literal double braces; a literal {{ or }} can also be escaped with a backslash.

PropertiesComponent has three scoped layers above the normal location-based lookup: override properties (highest priority, used first if the key exists), local (thread-local) properties (also take precedence and are used first if present — intended for test isolation without touching the shared properties file), and initial properties, which are added before any configured location is loaded, so they act as a base default a location file can override rather than a value that wins.

In a plain camel-main application (no Spring Boot or Quarkus), OS environment variables and JVM system properties can each participate in resolving any {{key}} automatically, controlled by camel.component.properties.environment-variable-mode and camel.component.properties.system-properties-mode, each settable to never (0), fallback (1, checked only if the key isn't resolvable elsewhere), or override (2, checked first, ahead of every configured location). Both default to override, and OS environment variable mode is checked before JVM system property mode, so the default effective order, highest to lowest, is: OS environment variable, JVM system property, then the configured location (e.g. a .properties file) — meaning an environment variable of the same key silently wins over a value written in a checked-in properties file by default.

On Spring Boot, Camel's {{...}} placeholders are bridged into Spring's own Environment abstraction, so they follow Spring Boot's externalized-configuration precedence rather than plain camel-main's: from highest to lowest, roughly, command-line arguments, JVM system properties, OS environment variables, profile-specific application-{profile}.properties/yml, then application.properties/yml, with the active profile selected by spring.profiles.active (or SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE). Notably, system properties outrank environment variables in Spring Boot's order, the opposite of camel-main's default (env before sys).

On Quarkus, Camel's {{...}} placeholders are backed by SmallRye Config (MicroProfile Config), whose sources are ranked by a numeric ordinal and consulted highest-ordinal-first: JVM system properties (ordinal 400), OS environment variables (300), and application.properties (250) are the three most common sources in a typical Camel Quarkus app, so — like Spring Boot, and unlike plain camel-main — a system property outranks an environment variable, which in turn outranks application.properties. A profile-specific value is written in the same file with a %profile-name. prefix (e.g. %prod.camel.component.kafka.brokers=...), and the active profile defaults to prod when packaged as a runnable jar, or dev/test under `quarkus:dev` and the test runner respectively.

Camel's vault property functions let a placeholder resolve directly from a cloud secrets manager instead of a local file: {{aws:secretName}} for AWS Secrets Manager, {{hashicorp:secret:path}} for HashiCorp Vault, and equivalents for Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager. Both AWS and HashiCorp syntaxes support a default (:default), a specific field within a JSON secret (#fieldName), and a specific version (@versionId); combined, AWS's form is {{aws:secretName#fieldName:defaultValue@versionId}} and HashiCorp's is {{hashicorp:secret:database#username:admin@2}}.

Each vault integration is a separate Maven dependency (camel-aws-secrets-manager, camel-hashicorp-vault, and so on) configured through camel.vault.<provider>.* properties or matching CAMEL_VAULT_<PROVIDER>_* environment variables — for AWS, either static accessKey/secretKey/region or defaultCredentialsProvider=true to use the standard AWS credential chain; for HashiCorp, token/host/port/scheme (plus hashicorp.cloud/namespace for HCP Vault).

Vault secrets can be kept in sync with the running CamelContext instead of only being read once at startup. AWS and Azure integrations lean on their platforms' own change-notification events (AWS via CloudTrail/EventBridge and an SQS queue, camel.vault.aws.useSqsNotification=true plus sqsQueueUrl; Azure via Event Grid); HashiCorp Vault has no native change-notification mechanism, so its integration instead polls the secret's metadata endpoint on an interval and compares the current_version field. Either mechanism requires camel.vault.<provider>.refreshEnabled=true, a comma-separated camel.vault.<provider>.secrets pattern naming which secrets to watch, a refreshPeriod in milliseconds for the polling case, and camel.main.context-reload-enabled=true so a detected change actually triggers Camel to reload the context (available since Camel 3.19).

The camel-kubernetes component exposes property functions that read directly from files Kubernetes mounts into the pod: {{configmap:name/key}} and the binary variant configmap-binary for ConfigMaps, {{secret:name/key}} and secret-binary for Secrets. These require the ConfigMap/Secret to actually be mounted as a volume in the pod spec (Camel reads it off local disk under the mount path, not via the Kubernetes API), so the function is only as current as the kubelet's propagation of a changed mounted Secret/ConfigMap to the pod's filesystem.

autoStartup accepts a property placeholder in every DSL — Java (.autoStartup("{{startupRouteProperty}}")), YAML (autoStartup: "{{integration.ftpEnabled}}"), and XML (<route autoStartup="{{key}}">) — and, combined with the ! negation prefix, a single boolean property can drive two routes in opposite directions, e.g. one route reads {{integration.ftpEnabled}} and a companion reads {{!integration.ftpEnabled}}, so exactly one of the pair is ever active. A route with autoStartup=false is still registered in the CamelContext, just not started; it can be started later at runtime by name through Camel's RouteController.

logMask (covered in the Observability chapter) and secret/credential placeholders address different halves of the same problem: logMask redacts sensitive header/property values in log output at runtime; property placeholders and vault functions keep the credential out of source control and out of the route definition in the first place. Neither substitutes for the other — a masked log line can still originate from a credential that was hardcoded in a URI string rather than externalized.

pitfalls: Assuming a checked-in .properties file always wins: under camel-main's own defaults (environment-variable-mode and system-properties-mode both default to override), an OS environment variable of the same key silently overrides a value from a configured location, before Camel even looks at the file. Spring Boot and Quarkus don't share this exact ordering — both put system properties above environment variables, the reverse of camel-main's default env-before-sys order — so a habit formed in one runtime can produce a genuinely different resolved value on another.

Leaving showAll=true on a log: endpoint, or interpolating a secret placeholder straight into a log() message template, defeats externalized secret management entirely — the value that was kept out of source control ends up in a log aggregator instead. logMask (Observability chapter) and keeping credentials in placeholders/vault functions are complementary controls, not substitutes for each other.

{{?key}} (optional) and {{key:default}} (placeholder default) are not the same thing: {{?key}} leaves the endpoint's own built-in default in force when the key is missing, while {{key:default}} substitutes a specific literal you chose; using {{?key}} where a specific fallback value is actually required silently falls back to whatever the component itself defaults to, which may not be the value intended.

A polling-based vault refresh (HashiCorp Vault, or AWS/Azure configured without their event-notification path) only detects a secret rotation on the next poll, not the instant it changes, and does nothing at all unless camel.main.context-reload-enabled=true is also set — refreshEnabled alone lets Camel notice the version changed, but reload-enabled is what actually acts on it.

A Kubernetes {{secret:name/key}} / {{configmap:name/key}} lookup reads a file Kubernetes mounted into the pod, not the Kubernetes API directly — if the volume was never mounted in the pod spec, or the app started before the kubelet finished propagating an updated Secret to the mounted file, the placeholder resolves against stale or missing data with no API-level error to point at the real cause.

claims.text: Camel Main (camel-main) is the lightweight, framework-free way to run a standalone Camel application: it boots a plain CamelContext from a main() method (or camel run via Camel JBang), with no Spring or Quarkus container underneath, and reads its configuration from application.properties using the same camel.main.* / camel.component.* property surface documented for the runtime.

A Spring Boot Camel application is packaged as a self-contained executable jar by the spring-boot-maven-plugin's repackage goal (bound to the Maven package phase once the plugin is declared in the POM), which nests the application's own classes plus all runtime dependencies inside one jar and adds a launcher so it runs with `java -jar app.jar`; adding the camel-spring-boot-starter dependency is what auto-configures a CamelContext as a Spring bean and auto-detects RouteBuilder beans on the classpath.

Camel Quarkus applications run in three distinct modes: dev mode (`mvn quarkus:dev`), which live-reloads route and Java changes on request and exposes the Dev UI; JVM mode, a runnable jar built with `mvn package` and started with `java -jar`, functionally similar to the Spring Boot jar; and native mode, built with `mvn package -Dnative` (or the native Maven profile), which ahead-of-time compiles the application to a platform-specific executable using GraalVM or its Quarkus-focused downstream distribution, Mandrel.

A native Quarkus/Camel executable trades a longer, more resource-hungry build (GraalVM native-image analysis of the whole closed-world class graph) for a dramatically faster, lighter runtime: startup measured in milliseconds rather than seconds, and resident memory in the tens of megabytes rather than hundreds — the trade that matters for serverless/FaaS-style integrations and container platforms that bill or autoscale on cold-start time and memory footprint.

Camel JBang's `camel run` command lets a route file (Java, YAML, or XML) run immediately with no Maven project, POM, or IDE — it resolves and downloads the Camel JARs and any components the route needs, and `--dev` adds live reload on file save; when a prototype is ready to productionize, `camel export --runtime=<spring-boot|quarkus|main>` turns the same route file(s) into a full Maven project scaffolded for that target runtime.

A CamelContext's lifecycle operations are build, init, start, stop, suspend, and resume (plus shutdown, the final teardown after stop). start/stop and suspend/resume are the two meaningful pairs: stop performs a full graceful shutdown of every route and releases resources, while suspend/resume only pauses and resumes consumers, keeping the CamelContext itself 'warm' — routes and their state stay registered, so resume is materially faster than a fresh start after stop.

Camel offers two RouteController implementations. The default controller is fail-fast: if any route throws during startup, CamelContext startup itself fails and the whole application refuses to come up. The SupervisingRouteController instead lets CamelContext start successfully even if some routes fail, and retries each failed route on an exponential backoff schedule in the background, so one route with a transiently-unreachable dependency (a database still booting, a broker not yet reachable) doesn't take down every other route in the application.

The supervising route controller is enabled with camel.routecontroller.enabled=true, and tuned with camel.routecontroller.backoff-delay (delay between retry attempts), camel.routecontroller.backoff-max-attempts (give up after N attempts; unset/0 means retry forever), camel.routecontroller.initial-delay, camel.routecontroller.thread-pool-size, and camel.routecontroller.include-routes / exclude-routes to scope which routes it supervises. As of Camel 4.7, a route that exhausts its retry attempts is (by default) marked unhealthy via the controller's unhealthy-on-exhausted behavior rather than silently disappearing, so a readiness probe wired to Camel's health checks will correctly report the application as not ready.

Camel's graceful shutdown is handled by a pluggable ShutdownStrategy (DefaultShutdownStrategy by default), triggered automatically when the CamelContext (or the surrounding Spring Boot/Quarkus application) stops — e.g. on SIGTERM from an orchestrator like Kubernetes. It shuts routes down in the reverse of their start order, and performs the shutdown in two phases: first a graceful phase that suspends/stops each route's consumers so no new work is accepted, while letting exchanges already in flight run to completion; then, if a configurable timeout (45 seconds by default) elapses before every route has drained, a forced phase that shuts the remaining routes down anyway.

The shutdown timeout and its related behavior are configured with camel.main.shutdown-timeout (default 45, in seconds), camel.main.shutdown-suppress-logging-on-timeout (quiet the forced-shutdown warning), and camel.main.log-inflight-exchanges-on-timeout (log which exchanges were still in flight when the timeout hit) — the same property names work in application.properties under plain camel-main, Spring Boot, and Quarkus. The strategy is also JMX-manageable at runtime, and setting the DefaultShutdownStrategy logger to DEBUG surfaces exactly which exchanges are still in-flight during a graceful shutdown.

Per-route shutdown behavior is tunable in the DSL with two enums: shutdownRoute(ShutdownRoute.Default | ShutdownRoute.Defer) — Default lets a route shut down as early as possible, while Defer delays shutting that route down to a later stage, for a route other routes still depend on (e.g. an internal direct: endpoint other routes send to); and shutdownRunningTask(ShutdownRunningTask.CompleteCurrentTaskOnly | ShutdownRunningTask.CompleteAllTasks) — CompleteCurrentTaskOnly finishes only the exchange currently being processed before stopping the consumer, while CompleteAllTasks (useful for a batch/file consumer mid-poll) lets the consumer finish every already-accepted task before stopping.

Camel also exposes shutting down (or restarting) a single named route programmatically via the CamelContext/RouteController API — e.g. shutdownRoute(routeId) or shutdownRoute(routeId, timeout, timeUnit) to override the default timeout for just that route — distinct from stopping the whole CamelContext.
